topicGaps: The 36.000-hour verified-video target remains unmet: 1 unique accessible specialty recording contributes 1.0911 observed hours (65:28); 34.9089 hours (34:54:32) remain. Scripted episodes and clip-plan target minutes are not rendered video and contribute zero hours.

Only units 1, 2, 5, 9 and 11 have the newly verified lecture mapped; units 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 12 have no verified external lecture from this expansion. The single recording is a broad introductory lecture, not comprehensive coverage of mapped units.

No publicly playable 36-hour institutional pediatric neuroradiology lecture archive was verified. ASPNR lists 31 free lectures, but the recording link leads to its member/e-learning area; login-free recording access and durations could not be established, so none counted.

Important insufficiently recorded domains remain: neonatal maturation and injury; trauma and separate suspected-abuse pathway; brain tumor protocols and response; infection/inflammation; cerebrovascular emergencies; detailed pediatric spine and cord; head-and-neck/orbit; metabolic/genetic patterns; protocol/safety/quality; age-specific normal development.

Five complete original teaching scripts are authored and source-mapped, but they are scripted only, not rendered or uploaded. Their content, nor the existing pilot or planned clip minutes, is not included in verified hours.

36 verified hours are not currently feasible from the verified public recording set. Closing the 34.9089-hour gap requires discovery and validation of additional unique open recordings or substantial original recording/production; this work does not establish feasibility or promise that source-backed material can fill the gap.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 9-year-old with minor blunt head trauma is assessed as high risk for clinically important brain injury by a validated pediatric rule. Which initial imaging study does ACR rate usually appropriate?

options.text: Skull radiographs
Noncontrast CT head
MRI with and without contrast
MRA head

practiceQuestions.rationale: For high-risk minor acute blunt pediatric head trauma (excluding suspected abusive head trauma), the ACR variant rates noncontrast head CT usually appropriate. Decisions remain clinician-led and follow local pathways; CT is not a universal response to every minor injury.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child has newly diagnosed nontraumatic seizures and is clinically stable. Which modality is generally preferred to evaluate structural causes?

options.text: Brain MRI without IV contrast
Routine skull radiographs
CT with IV contrast as first-line in every case
FDG-PET/CT

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR states MRI is more sensitive for brain abnormalities and is usually appropriate for new-onset seizures unrelated to trauma; emergency presentation and individual circumstances can change the pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A neonate is referred for imaging after seizures. Which statement best reflects ACR guidance for initial imaging?

options.text: MRI without contrast is usually appropriate; cranial US may be appropriate
CT angiography is always mandatory
Skull radiographs are the preferred test
No imaging is appropriate in neonates

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACR neonatal seizure variant lists MRI head without IV contrast as usually appropriate and cranial US as may be appropriate. Selection depends on clinical context and availability.

practiceQuestions.stem: A term neonate undergoing MRI for encephalopathy has diffusion restriction in a pattern concerning for hypoxic-ischemic injury. What is the safest interpretive next step?

options.text: Assign exact timing and prognosis from DWI alone
Describe distribution and timing-sensitive limitations; correlate with clinical course and sequence timing
Call it pathognomonic for a specific genetic disorder
Ignore conventional sequences

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neonatal HIE interpretation is pattern- and timing-dependent. DWI is valuable but must be interpreted with sequence timing, conventional images, clinical history and evolution; imaging alone should not determine exact injury timing or outcome.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a child with possible inflammatory white-matter disease, which principle is most defensible?

options.text: One imaging sign establishes a specific antibody diagnosis
Describe distribution and enhancement/diffusion features, then integrate clinical/laboratory context
Ignore age and developmental myelination
Use CT alone to exclude all inflammation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patterns help structure differential diagnosis but do not prove a specific immune or infectious cause. Age, evolution, clinical and laboratory findings matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about pediatric neuroradiology board certification is accurate in the United States ABR framework?

options.text: ABR awards a separate Pediatric Neuroradiology subspecialty certificate
ABR lists neuroradiology and pediatric radiology subspecialty pathways; this fellowship title itself is not a separate ABR certificate
Completion of any self-study course confers pediatric radiology eligibility
The ACR issues physician board certificates

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR describes neuroradiology and pediatric radiology as separate subspecialty certifications. ASPNR says there is no ACGME accreditation in pediatric neuroradiology as a subspecialty. The fellowship is an institutional clinical physician fellowship, not a separate board credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: For pediatric tumor imaging, which report statement is most appropriate when imaging overlaps across histologies?

options.text: State histology as proven by MRI alone
Describe compartment, signal, enhancement, diffusion and relevant staging findings; rank differential and recommend tissue/clinical correlation
Omit uncertainty from the report
Recommend therapy from this learning module

practiceQuestions.rationale: Imaging can narrow the differential and support staging but often cannot establish histology. A structured description and appropriate correlation is the defensible educational approach.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric patient with acute focal neurologic deficit is being evaluated for cerebrovascular disease. Which is the best imaging approach?

options.text: A single modality is always correct regardless of presentation
Use a time-critical institutional stroke pathway; select CT/CTA or MRI/MRA based on clinical state, availability, and the specific diagnostic question
Wait for outpatient imaging in every case
Use catheter angiography as screening in all cases

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR criteria address multiple procedures and clinical variants; urgent decisions depend on presentation, local resources and the question. Imaging education does not replace a pediatric stroke protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has developmental ventriculomegaly and abnormal myelination. What is the primary interpretive caution?

options.text: Use adult normal anatomy without adjustment
Account for age-dependent maturation and correlate with chronology and other findings
Call any T2 signal abnormality infection
Assume one sign identifies a syndrome

practiceQuestions.rationale: Normal brain signal and myelination change substantially with age; developmental stage and pattern distribution are central to pediatric interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching file includes authentic CT/MR images. What may a learner do under this course’s resource policy?

options.text: Download and republish images because the website is public
Use images for private study only where allowed by site terms; link to source, do not rehost/copy, and verify permission before reuse
Remove patient identifiers and freely redistribute
Use screenshots in a public course without license review

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not permission to reproduce. This course links to resources and requires compliance with repository conditions; no images or patient records are copied.

topicGaps: 36 verified free, directly playable external lecture hours remain unavailable at this check; all planned original clips remain planned, not ready or counted.

Need verifiable free video hours across pediatric neuroradiology, body, chest/cardiac, fetal/neonatal, GU, MSK, trauma/child protection, nuclear/molecular imaging, IR, quality/reporting, and communication.
ABR published guide is marked last verified 2017 and non-exhaustive; current official exam resources/blueprint should be rechecked.
AAR site lecture-player runtime/free playback not confirmed in this stateless review.

Actual verified public free external specialty media totals 6.1203 h (22,033 seconds); 29.8797 h remains to the 36-hour target. Authored scripts and clip plans remain unrendered and do not reduce the video-hour gap.

The counted open lectures concentrate on pediatric MRI technical/protocol pitfalls and the pediatric IR interface; they do not supply a complete image-rich interpretation course. No verifiable long-form recordings were counted for neonatal brain or chest radiograph interpretation, routine ultrasound technique, common GU, fetal, cardiac, nuclear/molecular, oncology, trauma/child-protection differentials or structured reporting/QA.

ABR study guide itself says last verified 2017 and non-exhaustive. Its three-domain map is historical only; the public 2026 exam guide is not a comprehensive published topic-by-topic blueprint. Map course coverage to the supplied broad headings, not invented exam weighting.

Institutional rotations and conference schedules do not disclose exact rotation lengths, case counts or complete lecture syllabi; the Hopkins and BCH public curriculum descriptions remain distinct institutional variants, not a single course.

Accessible ACR appendicitis criteria page is explicitly marked New 2018. Use it as a dated reasoning demonstration only; re-check the current ACR version and local policy before any clinical application.

Clinical signs and pathways for skeletal survey, neonatal emergencies, contrast/sedation, nuclear imaging, child safety, procedures and treatment require contemporary specialist guidance and supervision. The brief episodes do not provide individual patient care, diagnosis, prescribing, procedure instructions, privileges, or abuse attribution.
Human clinician review remains not performed; no accredited teaching, supervised image interpretation, clinical competence, eligibility or examination readiness is established.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship subspecialty (independent self-study; not a training programme)
boardNames: American Board of Radiology (ABR) Pediatric Radiology subspecialty certification
American Osteopathic Board of Radiology (AOBR) Pediatric Radiology subspecialty certification

boardStatus.ABR: Separate Pediatric Radiology subspecialty exam/certificate exists; usual route requires primary ABR general radiology, diagnostic radiology, or IR/DR specialty certificate and one post-residency year in an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited pediatric radiology fellowship. The ABR page also describes alternate pathways and a 15-month DR-resident pathway. Eligibility rules are board-controlled and change; verify individually.
boardStatus.AOBR: Separate osteopathic Pediatric Radiology subspecialty exam exists; official page requires primary AOBR Diagnostic Radiology certification and one-year AOA-recognized or ACGME-accredited fellowship. Verify eligibility directly.
boardStatus.Institutional distinction: The two named offerings are pediatric radiology physician fellowships, not distinct board examinations or one combined Harvard/JHU course. JHU also describes an additional focused ACGME Advanced Specialty Training year in pediatric neuroradiology/fetal MR, and BCH describes possible further focused subspecialty/research years; these are not counted as additional pediatric radiology board tracks here. A 15-month ABR pathway is an alternative within diagnostic-radiology residency, not a joint institutional degree.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: An independent course cannot award prerequisites, accredited training time, board eligibility, exam access, or certification. Eligibility and examination requirements are determined only by ABR/AOBR/RCPSC as applicable. No pass guarantee.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Children’s Center
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Radiology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page states a one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship with one accredited position. Body CT/MR/US/fluoroscopy/radiography plus inpatient/outpatient, ED, nursery, NICU/PICU and oncology exposure; additional neuroradiology, fetal MR, nuclear/molecular imaging and IR rotations; daily clinical/subspecialty conferences and academic time. It also describes an additional ACGME Advanced Specialty Training year for qualified fellows in pediatric neuroradiology/fetal MR. Exact rotation duration/case counts are not published.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Radiology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page states first year fully ACGME-accredited for up to 10 fellows. One-year clinical rotation list: body CT/MR, MSK, neuro, fetal/neonatal, NMMI, US, fluoroscopy, IR and ED; twice-daily lectures/conferences; one academic project expected. Further focused subspecialty/research opportunities may follow. Exact schedule/case counts not published.

officialProgrammes.name: Mass General Brigham Pediatric Radiology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact institutional variants retained from task packet: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine/Johns Hopkins Children’s Center and Boston Children’s Hospital. Public programme pages, rather than generic directory categories, establish the clinical physician subspecialty. Fellowship status is reported as stated on the institution pages; it was not independently matched against an individual live ACGME ADS record. No research-only or nonphysician programme is included. Pediatric neuroradiology, pediatric VIR, diagnostic/nuclear medical physics residency and Informatics are separate programmes/tracks and excluded.
sourceCaveats: ACGME requirements page lists pediatric radiology program requirements effective 2026-07-01; their existence does not independently prove a specific program’s current accreditation. Named institution pages themselves state ACGME accreditation.
ABR study-guide PDF is dated as last verified 2017; ABR certification page and the 2026 exam guide were fetched, but candidate-specific eligibility must be confirmed directly.
ACR appendicitis webpage displayed “New 2018” and needs current-version confirmation before clinical use.
BCH page includes forward application dates for 2028–29, demonstrating the page is maintained, but those dates are not used as board requirements.
YouTube playlist direct media playback could not be checked without encountering a sign-in/bot-verification challenge; no authentication workaround attempted.
The IAEA package link, WHO PDF link, and AAR videos were not downloaded or locally inspected.
No human clinical review performed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical child is assessed as low clinical risk for appendicitis. Based on the ACR child-specific appropriateness page fetched here, which answer best reflects its current displayed variant?

options.text: Routine CT abdomen/pelvis is usually appropriate.
Initial imaging is generally not recommended for low-risk children.
Every child should undergo ultrasound followed by CT.
MRI with and without contrast is required.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The displayed low-risk variant rates abdominal US, CT, MRI and radiography as usually not appropriate. The ACR page identifies itself as new 2018, so check for updates; no generic recommendation replaces current clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a child with intermediate clinical risk of appendicitis, the retrieved ACR narrative rates which initial option “Usually Appropriate”?

options.text: Right-lower-quadrant ultrasound
Abdominal radiography
CT without and with IV contrast
Pelvic ultrasound only

practiceQuestions.rationale: In the page’s intermediate-risk variant, abdominal or RLQ ultrasound is usually appropriate; other options are conditional or not appropriate. Confirm the current revision and local pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric X-ray/CT protocol is being planned. Which principle aligns with FDA guidance?

options.text: Use adult settings to maintain a uniform image appearance.
Choose technique for the patient’s size and clinical question, using the lowest dose that provides adequate diagnostic image quality.
Avoid all X-ray studies in children regardless of benefit.
Use age alone and ignore patient size.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA stresses size-adjusted technique and the lowest dose adequate for diagnosis/intervention; needed imaging benefits can exceed the small individual risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: An appropriate non-ionizing exam can answer the same clinical question. What is an appropriate first consideration?

options.text: Order both tests routinely.
Consider US or MRI as appropriate and avoid duplicate imaging.
Prefer CT because it is faster in every case.
Do not review prior imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA recommends considering equally useful ultrasound or MRI when appropriate and checking history to avoid duplicates; not every alternative is diagnostically interchangeable.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is within the three broad areas in the ABR pediatric radiology guide retrieved for this review?

options.text: Breast, cardiac electrophysiology and adult trauma.
Chest/cardiac/facial bones/ENT/airway; MSK/spine/CNS; GI/GU/interventional.
Only abdominal ultrasound.
Obstetric ultrasound only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are the guide’s three broad groupings. The same PDF says its outline is general and non-exhaustive, and it was last verified in 2017.

practiceQuestions.stem: What primary credential and training does the ABR page state for the usual pediatric radiology subspecialty certification route?

options.text: Any medical degree and any online course.
ABR general radiology, diagnostic radiology or IR/DR specialty certificate plus one year ACGME/RCPSC-accredited pediatric radiology fellowship.
Pediatric residency alone.
No prerequisite specialty certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This is the listed usual ABR route. Alternative pathways and the 15-month residency pathway have their own conditions. An independent course confers none of these.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the AOBR official page, the osteopathic pediatric radiology exam pathway requires which prerequisite?

options.text: Primary AOBR Diagnostic Radiology certification and one-year AOA-recognized or ACGME-accredited fellowship.
ABR certification only.
A research doctorate.
No fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AOBR describes its own certification path and annual exam; it is separate from ABR. Eligibility must be confirmed with the board.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public pediatric case is selected from Radiopaedia for a classroom. Which condition should be observed before reusing its image?

options.text: No attribution if publicly visible.
Follow its CC BY-NC-SA conditions, attribute the case/contributor and rID, use noncommercially, and share adapted material alike.
Remove attribution and place behind a paid course.
Assume free viewing grants redistribution rights.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia says the case content is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, with attribution and same-license conditions and noncommercial limits; linking is safer than copying.

options.text: Its one-year pediatric radiology fellowship is ACGME-accredited, with an additional focused year available for qualified fellows.
The listed course itself confers ABR eligibility.
Every fellowship is two years.
The program awards an AOBR certificate.

options.text: A complete, current board blueprint verified in 2026.

A licensed set of case images.

title: Pediatric Vascular and Interventional Radiology Fellowship
prerequisites: Physician-level intended audience: diagnostic radiology board certification/equivalent and prior pediatric or interventional radiology fellowship are the prerequisites stated on the BCH fellowship page; the course itself does not qualify applicants.
Knowledge of pediatric and adult imaging modalities, basic vascular anatomy, IR indications, radiology physics, radiation protection, and clinical communication.
Non-physician learners may study concepts but must not interpret clinical studies, make patient-care decisions, or perform procedures.
objectives: Use current ISSVA terminology and distinguish vascular tumors, malformations and named-vessel developmental anomalies.
Correlate clinical history and examination with ultrasound/Doppler and MRI/MRA/MRV patterns while stating uncertainty.
Explain pediatric-specific imaging, radiation, anesthesia, consent/assent and multidisciplinary safety considerations.
Compare the broad conceptual scope of vascular and nonvascular pediatric interventions, alternatives, complications and follow-up.
Reason from source evidence and communicate observation separately from inference.
Map learning to broad ABR IR/DR content domains without claiming an official pediatric IR exam blueprint.

units.title: Scope, pathway and systems of pediatric IR
objectives: Distinguish the named BCH one-year fellowship from accredited DR/IR residency and from pediatric radiology subspecialty certification.
Frame an IR consult as a multidisciplinary question, not a procedure request alone.
topics: scope and institution variants; consult/referral; shared decision making; limits of public programme descriptions
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Noninterpretive Skills
units.casePractice: Open a linked case only as an external learning example; separate known facts from missing history and consult questions. No patient record is copied.
units.assessment: One-page pathway map and 150-word consult response: identify prerequisites, options, uncertainty and who must join the team.

units.title: Pediatric imaging, radiation and periprocedural safety
objectives: Explain why age, body size, growth, anesthesia and developmental context change imaging/procedure planning.
Identify dose-optimization questions and communication checkpoints without prescribing settings or doses.
topics: US-first question formulation; fluoroscopy/CT/DSA exposure; ALARA and dose monitoring; contrast/sedation/anesthesia coordination; consent and assent; time-out and handoff
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Physics; Noninterpretive Skills; Interventional Radiology
units.casePractice: For each linked example, create a modality/safety checklist without extracting patient identifiers or recommending treatment.
units.assessment: Safety worksheet scored for modality justification, risk/benefit, radiation-minimization questions, consent/assent and escalation triggers.

units.title: Vascular anomaly classification and terminology
objectives: Apply the current ISSVA structure: vascular tumors, malformations (fast-flow, slow-flow, named-vessel developmental anomalies), and potentially unique vascular anomalies.
Avoid treating “hemangioma,” “AVM,” “vascular tumor” and “malformation” as interchangeable labels.
topics: 2025 ISSVA living classification and glossary; clinical history; flow; Doppler; developmental/syndromic context; limitations of older teaching videos
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Pediatric Radiology; Interventional Radiology
units.casePractice: Compare a de-identified externally hosted vascular anomaly case description with the ISSVA glossary; do not infer histology from one image.
units.assessment: Classification exercise: provisional nomenclature with “what remains uncertain”; rubric rewards current terminology and differential, not certainty.

units.title: Imaging work-up and preprocedural planning for vascular anomalies
objectives: Choose the imaging question and describe complementary roles/limits of ultrasound, Doppler, MRI/MRA/MRV and catheter angiography.
Summarize extent, flow pattern, critical structures and multidisciplinary consultation needs.
topics: clinical exam and imaging correlation; flow voids; lesion extent; airway, orbital, neural, bone and organ relationships; protocol decisions; limits of angiography
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Pediatric Radiology; Interventional Radiology; Physics
units.casePractice: Use an external Radiopaedia search case or review figure: write observation vs inference columns and list what an image cannot settle.
units.assessment: Structured imaging report assessed for anatomy, modality rationale, flow language, differential, limits and next question.

units.title: Slow-flow venous and lymphatic malformations: intervention concepts
objectives: Explain how lesion type, symptoms, extent, coagulopathy and proximity to critical structures inform multidisciplinary treatment discussion.
Compare sclerotherapy, observation, medical/surgical options at a conceptual level without giving agent doses or procedural instructions.
topics: venous and lymphatic malformation categories; macrocystic/microcystic pattern; venography; sclerosant classes at conceptual level; complications and follow-up; uncertainty
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology
units.casePractice: Review an authentic linked case, identify which data support slow-flow versus alternatives, then document unresolved risks rather than recommending a procedure.
units.assessment: Decision memo with differential, goals, alternatives, risk context, team members and follow-up questions. No drug/dose choices.

units.title: Fast-flow AVM/AVF and embolization reasoning
objectives: Differentiate fast-flow from slow-flow patterns and describe the nidus/shunt concept without reducing complex anomalies to a single finding.
Recognize why non-target embolization and adjacent critical anatomy require expert supervised care.
topics: AVM/AVF classification; Doppler/MRA/angiography; referral and treatment planning; embolization routes/agents as categories; staged care and complications
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology; Physics
units.casePractice: Analyze linked educational case descriptions; list observations, hypotheses and red flags requiring multidisciplinary review. Do not simulate procedural steps.
units.assessment: Annotated differential and hazard map with source citations, uncertainty labels and one alternative management pathway.

units.title: Lymphatic anomalies, lymphangiography and leaks
objectives: Describe congenital lymphatic malformation versus acquired lymphatic leak as different problem categories.
Compare diagnostic imaging concepts and multidisciplinary options while avoiding procedure authorization.
topics: macrocystic/microcystic lesions; complex lymphatic anomalies; central conducting anomalies; MR/fluoroscopic lymphangiography concepts; leaks and post-cardiac-surgery context
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology
units.casePractice: Use open review images/text by link only; outline the information needed to localize a leak and distinguish alternative causes.
units.assessment: Short case discussion: pathophysiology, image question, options, risks and team members; no copied images.

units.title: Venous access, pediatric thrombosis and venous intervention
objectives: Compare common pediatric access-device needs and complications using size, access preservation and lifetime vascular health concepts.
Summarize thrombosis assessment and referral logic without substituting for current hematology/IR guidelines.
topics: US-guided access; central access devices; catheter dysfunction; venous thrombosis; thrombolysis/thrombectomy concepts; filters and retrieval; follow-up
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology; Noninterpretive Skills
units.casePractice: From a linked educational case, create a problem representation and list the missing laboratory/imaging/clinical data; no line placement instruction.
units.assessment: Access/thrombosis concept map scored for indication, alternatives, complications, collaboration and safety limits.

units.title: Arterial interventions and pediatric trauma
objectives: Distinguish observation, surgery and catheter-based intervention as team decisions grounded in stability, anatomy and current pediatric trauma evidence.
Explain why adult thresholds and historic case anecdotes cannot be imported uncritically.
topics: traumatic hemorrhage; iatrogenic injury; renal/portal/hepatic/pulmonary/bronchial arteries; angioplasty/embolization categories; non-target ischemia; evidence limitations
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology; Physics
units.casePractice: Review the 2018 lecture as dated educational context and compare a case narrative with current institutional/pediatric trauma guidance before drawing conclusions.
units.assessment: Evidence critique: separate old numerical claims from current standards; write a neutral team-handoff summary.

units.title: Nonvascular interventions: biopsy, drainage and enteric access
objectives: Describe the clinical decision framework for image-guided biopsy and drainage, including alternatives, sample needs and follow-up.
Explain pediatric adaptation and team dependencies for enteric/feeding access.
topics: US/CT/fluoroscopy question selection; biopsy planning; fluid collection; pleural/empyema; gastrostomy/GJ/cecostomy; pediatric anesthesia, aftercare and complications
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology; Noninterpretive Skills
units.casePractice: Use one externally linked authentic case or open review and identify target, safe-window questions, expected specimen and competing options.
units.assessment: Imaging-guided intervention planning worksheet: indication, alternatives, sample/tube needs, follow-up, and risk/communication checklist.

units.title: Biliary, GU, transplant and pediatric oncology interventions
objectives: Explain how imaging-guided access, biopsy, drainage, ablation and transplant-related procedures are selected collaboratively.
Recognize age-specific anatomy, tissue-sparing goals and evidence limits in rare pediatric disease.
topics: biliary obstruction/stricture; nephrostomy and urinary obstruction; transplant vascular complications; tumor biopsy/ablation; thermal ablation concepts; pediatric oncology conferences
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology
units.casePractice: Use open-access case/review material as a link and prepare a differential plus questions for surgery, oncology, anesthesia and pathology.
units.assessment: Five-minute oral-board style case summary: problem, imaging, options, hazards, limits and escalation. Original scenario only.

units.title: Integration, quality, communication and board-cognitive review
objectives: Use an observation–interpretation–decision structure to synthesize a pediatric IR case.
Map review to ABR IR/DR general domains while recognizing there is no pediatric IR-specific exam blueprint.
topics: case conference; complications/M&M; consent/assent; radiation safety; QI; literature appraisal; uncertainty; original practice questions
boardDomains: ABR IR/DR: Interventional Radiology; Pediatric Radiology; Noninterpretive Skills; Physics
units.casePractice: Synthesize two public, de-identified case-resource pages as links only; note source permissions and do not download, reproduce or submit patient records.
units.assessment: Final portfolio: oral case, source appraisal and 10 original questions. Formative only; no cut score or pass prediction.

assignment.title: Pediatric IR multidisciplinary case-conference portfolio
deliverables: Two externally linked authentic case-resource reviews, with no images or patient records copied. Verify de-identification, case rights and current terminology.
One structured vascular anomaly work-up: clinical questions, observations, provisional ISSVA category, differential, modality purpose and uncertainty.
One nonvascular or vascular access case summary with indication, alternatives, team roles and follow-up questions.
A one-page critique of a public pediatric IR recording against current primary/authoritative sources, dated and qualified.
assignment.scoring: Five criteria scored 0–4 (0 absent/unsafe, 1 major omissions, 2 partial, 3 sound, 4 precise and well-supported); weight equally to 100. Formative education only; no clinical credentialing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lesion is referred as a “hemangioma,” but the referral lacks age of onset, growth history and flow characterization. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Accept hemangioma as a complete diagnosis and schedule treatment.
Clarify clinical history/exam and use current ISSVA terminology while characterizing imaging features.
Assume every congenital lesion is an AVM.
Use biopsy as the default first step for all vascular anomalies.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The label is nonspecific. Clinical course and imaging should be correlated, and current ISSVA classification distinguishes tumors and malformations with finer categories. No single finding mandates intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a superficial pediatric vascular anomaly, which imaging statement is most accurate?

options.text: Ultrasound with Doppler can provide useful initial flow/architecture information without ionizing radiation, but MRI may be needed for extent and deep relationships.
CT is always the first-line modality.
MRI is never useful once Doppler is performed.
Catheter angiography is required to classify every lesion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ultrasound/Doppler and MRI can answer complementary questions; modality choice depends on the clinical problem and lesion extent.

practiceQuestions.stem: A current classification update divides vascular malformations chiefly into which broad groups?

options.text: Benign, borderline, malignant only.
Fast-flow, slow-flow and developmental anomalies of named vessels.
Arterial, venous, lymphatic only with no combined group.
Congenital and acquired only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 updated ISSVA classification uses fast-flow, slow-flow and developmental anomalies of named vessels as principal malformation groupings; consult the live official table for detail.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source should control terminology when an older educational video uses a different vascular anomaly taxonomy?

options.text: Anecdotal consensus from that video.
The current official ISSVA Classification and Glossary, with its update date.
A search snippet.
A single online image caption.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Older lectures may be useful but the official living ISSVA resource is the canonical current classification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child has a complex lesion near critical anatomy. What is the most defensible educational next step before discussing intervention?

options.text: Choose a sclerosant based on the lesion name alone.
Describe imaging extent/flow and convene appropriate multidisciplinary review, noting uncertainties and alternatives.
Apply adult procedure thresholds directly.
Promise a curative procedure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Treatment depends on type, extent, symptoms, location and team assessment; education must not create certainty or competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source fact is valid for the Boston Children’s fellowship as currently posted?

options.text: It is a board examination.
It is a one-year institutional fellowship and requires DR board certification/equivalent plus a prior pediatric or IR fellowship.
It is an ACGME-accredited residency.
It guarantees eligibility for pediatric radiology certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BCH page states one year and those candidate prerequisites. It does not say the fellowship itself is ACGME-accredited or guarantee eligibility for a separate certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about board certification is accurate for this track?

options.text: A separate ABR Pediatric Interventional Radiology subspecialty exam exists.
ABR offers Pediatric Radiology subspecialty certification and IR/DR certification, but no separate pediatric IR exam was listed on current ABR pages.
Completing this curriculum grants ABR eligibility.
Pediatric IR is an ABMS board on its own.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR public pages describe pediatric radiology subspecialty certification and IR/DR specialty certification, without a separate pediatric IR certificate/exam; eligibility depends on board rules and accredited training, not this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric IR webinar presents institutional procedure numbers and practice patterns from 2018. How should they be used?

options.text: As current universal standards.
As historical context that must be checked against current evidence and local pediatric protocols.
As a substitute for guidelines.
As proof of fellowship eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single older webinar is not a current standard or universal practice guideline.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the proper way to use Radiopaedia cases in an independent study course?

options.text: Download all images because cases are free to view.
Link to the external case and verify its de-identification, case-specific rights and license; do not copy/rehost absent permission.
Remove attribution and reuse figures.
Assume all images are public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 with attribution/share-alike/noncommercial conditions; free viewing does not equal unrestricted reuse.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which describes the ABR exam mapping in this curriculum?

options.text: An official pediatric IR exam blueprint.
An educational mapping to broad ABR IR/DR domains; it is not a pediatric IR-specific board blueprint.
A guarantee of passing all boards.
A replacement for ABR study guides.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR publishes IR/DR domains and pediatric radiology subspecialty certification, but no pediatric IR blueprint was found. This mapping is formative only.

title: Radiology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship directory category / multi-track independent educational course-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Post-core radiology self-study for physicians/advanced imaging learners. Assumes medical anatomy, basic pathology, modality fundamentals and familiarity with an interpreted radiology report. Not a first course in medicine and not an alternative to accredited residency/fellowship.
recommendedPreparation: Read the open imaging fundamentals chapters on modality physics and anatomy.
Review basic CT attenuation/reconstruction, MRI contrast, ultrasound artifacts, contrast safety and radiation protection.
Identify the applicable current ACR topic and local clinical escalation policy before interpreting any clinical material.
excludedCompetencies: No patient care, independent report sign-off, image-guided procedure, radiation-safety authorization, supervised case volume or competence attestation.

objectives: Use indication, appropriateness, technical adequacy and safety to frame imaging interpretation.
Apply modality-aware search patterns and separate observations, differential diagnoses and uncertainty.

Recognize common imaging patterns across BIDMC’s listed fellowship tracks and map learning to published ABR DR Core and neuroradiology domains without presenting the course as an official board blueprint.
Select openly accessible readings and authentic case links while following copyright, de-identification, attribution and no-rehosting rules.
Communicate limitations, critical findings and recommendations for appropriate human-supervised follow-up.

units.title: Clinical imaging decisions, safety, and communication
objectives: Translate a clinical question into the minimum sufficient imaging pathway and state why alternatives may be unsuitable.
Identify contrast, pregnancy, radiation, MRI safety, and communication issues requiring escalation.
Write a concise impression that distinguishes finding, differential, uncertainty, and urgency.
topics: ACR Appropriateness Criteria as scenario guidance
Structured report quality and error reflection
units.casePractice: Use an ACR topic scenario and linked case only; justify modality/next-step choice with uncertainty statement.
units.assessment: 5-item appropriateness/safety quiz plus one revised impression; rubric: indication match 40%, safety caveats 25%, uncertainty 20%, clarity 15%.

units.title: Image formation, CT physics, and technical quality
objectives: Relate attenuation, reconstruction, windowing, spatial resolution, noise, and dose to image appearance.
Recognize common acquisition artifacts and describe their diagnostic limitations.
Explain why protocol parameters depend on the question rather than routine multiphase imaging.
topics: Contrast timing as task-specific protocol design
units.casePractice: Annotate one public CT case for phase, artifact, and limitation; do not download its images.
units.assessment: One-page protocol critique; rubric: correctly identifies technical limitation 35%, dose/contrast tradeoff 30%, alternative protocol 25%, citation 10%.

units.title: MRI principles, sequence selection, and body MRI workflow
objectives: Distinguish T1/T2-weighted, diffusion, susceptibility, perfusion, and fat-suppressed contrasts at a conceptual level.
Describe how indication, field strength/safety, motion, and contrast contraindications constrain a protocol.
Separate sequence signal behavior from a disease-specific interpretation.
topics: Motion, chemical shift, metal and field inhomogeneity
units.casePractice: Use a public neuro or body MRI case to map each sequence to the question; no procedure instructions.
units.assessment: Sequence-matching worksheet and 3-minute oral explanation; rubric: sequence rationale 40%, signal reasoning 30%, artifacts 20%, safety 10%.

units.title: Ultrasound, radiography, and cross-sectional modality integration
objectives: Compare ultrasound, radiography, CT, MRI, and PET/CT by spatial/temporal resolution, tissue contrast, radiation, and limitations.
Construct a modality comparison for one fictional clinical indication without turning it into a treatment directive.
Identify when a focused ultrasound examination cannot resolve the clinical question.
units.casePractice: Compare modalities using ACR topic materials and a public case page; case findings are not copied.
units.assessment: Modality matrix; rubric: appropriate strengths 40%, limits 30%, safety 20%, readable rationale 10%.

units.title: Neuroradiology: acute brain and vascular imaging
objectives: Apply a systematic CT/MRI review to emergency brain imaging and localize a visible abnormality.
Explain the complementary roles and limits of CT, CTA, DWI/ADC, and perfusion in suspected ischemia.
State when imaging observations need urgent communication without issuing treatment orders.
topics: Hemorrhage, edema, mass effect, herniation language
Acute ischemia, vessel imaging, DWI/ADC/perfusion concepts
units.casePractice: Public Radiopaedia neuro case search; write localization, differential, urgency, and one explicit limitation.
units.assessment: Timed image-description worksheet; rubric: systematic review 25%, localization 30%, differential 25%, critical communication 20%.

units.title: Neuroradiology: spine, head and neck, tumor, infection
objectives: Use anatomic compartments and pattern description to organize brain, spine, and head/neck differentials.
Compare sequence and modality contributions in mass, infection, and degenerative scenarios.
Separate imaging description from tissue diagnosis and avoid false certainty.
topics: Brain lesion compartments and enhancement patterns
Spine marrow, canal, and cord localization
Infection, tumor, vascular and inflammatory differentials
units.casePractice: Use case library filters for brain/spine/head-neck. For each selected case capture the case DOI/link and page-specific rights note, not images.
units.assessment: Two differential-building exercises; rubric: anatomic localization 30%, useful differential 30%, modality reasoning 25%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Abdominal imaging and image-guided care boundaries
objectives: Choose CT/MRI/US/fluoroscopy approaches conceptually for abdominal questions using current ACR criteria.
Interpret phases and cross-sectional anatomy at a teaching level and state key uncertainty.
Distinguish observing a procedure and understanding its indication from procedural competency.
topics: Liver, pancreas, biliary, adrenal, renal and GU protocol concepts
units.casePractice: Use abdominal case library or ACR scenario and report the clinical question, modality limits, and differential.
units.assessment: Protocol-selection memo; rubric: indication 30%, protocol choice 25%, differential 25%, safety/escalation 20%.

units.title: Body MRI, pelvic/GU, and classification systems
objectives: Describe a systematic body MRI read and sequence-specific findings without substituting classification for diagnosis.
Select the applicable organ-specific lexicon and avoid cross-applying PI-RADS, LI-RADS, and renal cystic lesion systems.
Communicate limitations such as motion, phase timing, or incomplete protocol.
topics: Liver and pancreas MRI; biliary sequences
Prostate/pelvic MRI overview and PI-RADS scope
Renal masses/cystic lesions require distinct classification
Enterography, rectal and pelvic MRI basics
units.casePractice: Choose one body MRI case and identify the organ-specific reporting framework from an authoritative source; do not infer a diagnosis from a label alone.
units.assessment: Classification-selection quiz; rubric: correct organ-system match 40%, sequence reasoning 25%, differential/limits 25%, source trace 10%.

units.title: Breast imaging and image-guided pathway reasoning
objectives: Describe screening versus diagnostic breast imaging at a high level and distinguish clinical presentations.
Use ACR topic recommendations as current scenario-based guidance, checking revision date and patient-specific qualifiers.
Explain why BI-RADS is breast-specific and why a teaching self-study cannot authorize biopsy or management.
topics: Breast density, screening limitations and communication
BI-RADS scope and need for current authorized edition
units.casePractice: Use a public breast case, if available, for description only; pair with ACR appropriateness topic and a page-specific licensing check.
units.assessment: Short case report and modality selection; rubric: clinical question 25%, modality rationale 35%, limitations 25%, citation 15%.

units.title: Cardiothoracic imaging
objectives: Apply a reproducible chest radiograph and CT search pattern and distinguish focal from diffuse patterns.
Describe cardiothoracic CT/MRI roles, protocol constraints and incidental findings without overcalling.
Recognize serial change and articulate why comparison studies may alter differential.
units.casePractice: Review the linked longitudinal lung case on source site; distinguish observed changes from diagnosis and avoid exporting images.
units.assessment: Serial comparison timeline plus structured impression; rubric: search pattern 25%, change detection 30%, alternative explanations 20%, limitations/communication 25%.

units.title: Musculoskeletal imaging and safe reporting
objectives: Use alignment, bone, cartilage/joint, soft tissue and neurovascular checks in a systematic MSK review.
Select modality conceptually for osseous versus marrow/soft-tissue questions and note trauma artifacts/limitations.
Describe findings without crossing into procedure competence or unsupported treatment direction.
topics: Radiographs, CT, MRI and ultrasound roles
Trauma, degenerative, infection and neoplasm patterns
units.casePractice: Use case repository MSK filters; describe one finding and differential with specific modality limitation.
units.assessment: Image-description station; rubric: systematic review 25%, localization 25%, differential 25%, limitations and wording 25%.

units.title: Cancer imaging, nuclear medicine, and integrated subspecialty practice
objectives: Explain structural versus functional imaging at a high level and recognize that radiotracer uptake is not histology.
Recognize common FDG PET/CT physiologic uptake, artifacts, false positives and false negatives; recommend correlation rather than unsupported certainty.
Summarize differences among BIDMC cancer imaging, cross-sectional, body MRI and nuclear radiology categories; do not invent a nuclear fellowship at BIDMC.
topics: Cancer imaging modality selection and staging context
PET/CT registration, physiologic uptake and interpretive pitfalls
Nuclear radiology board status versus BIDMC fellowship offerings
Consultation, multidisciplinary conferences, QI and evidence update habits
units.casePractice: Analyze an openly linked PET/CT case or public case library item with correlation and limitation notes; no therapy/dose decisions.
units.assessment: PET/CT pitfall case memo; rubric: modality reasoning 25%, uptake interpretation 30%, alternatives/correlation 25%, safety/uncertainty 20%.

assignment.title: Integrated multimodality case conference memo (fictional case only)
assignment.instructions: Select a public case page for independent viewing or write a clearly fictional scenario. Do not copy its images or patient record. Deliver a 1–2 page note with indication, modality choice, search pattern, observation, top differential, limitation, communication priority, and one current source. Keep description separate from diagnosis and management.
assignment.passRule: Educational self-check only: 80% suggests revisiting missed areas; it is not validated or equivalent to board performance.

assessment.format: 12-unit self-study; diagnostic pretest; short low-stakes checks; two written case memos; final mixed-domain question set. Original questions here are not copied from protected ABR items.

studyHours.breakdown: 36 target viewing hours (only 2.5658 hours currently verified), 54 hours reading/notes, 54 hours linked case observation and written interpretation, 24 hours retrieval practice/reflection. The 168-hour figure is a proposed self-study plan, not a residency/fellowship training-hours claim.
studyHours.weeklyPlan: 12 weeks × 14 planned study hours; adapt to learner background.

assessment.completion: Course completion means only self-reported completion of this independent course; it confers no credit, certificate, patient-care authority or exam readiness.

American Board of Radiology (ABR) — Nuclear Radiology, Pediatric Radiology and Pain Medicine subspecialty certificates are current ABR categories but no corresponding BIDMC nuclear/pediatric fellowship is listed in this umbrella directory
medical.boardStatus: No single examination or certifying board corresponds to the BIDMC category-level label “Radiology Fellowship.” The ABR Diagnostic Radiology Core exam is a residency-level breadth reference, not a fellowship credential. Current ABR subspecialty certification pathways/exams include neuroradiology, nuclear radiology, pediatric radiology and pain medicine. Of the exact eight BIDMC fellowship labels retained here, only Neuroradiology maps directly to the described ABR subspecialty exam. Nuclear and pediatric fellowships are not listed in the BIDMC directory; body MRI, cancer imaging, cross-sectional imaging, breast imaging, cardiothoracic imaging and MSK imaging do not each have a separate current ABR subspecialty exam under these names. ACGME programme accreditation is not board certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course grants no ABR eligibility. ABR primary Diagnostic Radiology certification requires the board’s current prior clinical training, accredited residency or approved alternate pathway, examinations, license and other criteria. ABR neuroradiology subspecialty eligibility requires a qualifying primary certificate, accredited neuroradiology fellowship and additional current requirements. Confirm the official board rules for the actual candidate and exam date; no guarantee of passing.

officialProgrammes.name: Abdominal imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory label; dedicated page calls it the Abdominal Imaging and Interventions Radiology Fellowship, one-year ACGME-accredited. Public curriculum lists supervised CT/MRI/US/fluoroscopy, cross-sectional interventions, call, conferences, QI/research/teaching. This independent course does not teach procedure competence.

officialProgrammes.name: Body MRI
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate one-year fellowship; public overview describes clinical and research MRI. Do not merge with Abdominal Imaging & Interventions.

officialProgrammes.name: Breast imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate one-year advanced fellowship in breast imaging; no distinct current ABR subspecialty exam listed for this named track.

officialProgrammes.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in collaboration with Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Cancer imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate one-year fellowship; public directory describes clinical interpretation of adult cancer imaging with MRI, CT, PET-CT and US. Dana-Farber collaboration preserved as stated.

officialProgrammes.name: Cardiothoracic imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate one-year fellowship with clinical, educational and research thoracic imaging activities. Not equated with cardiovascular imaging board certification.

officialProgrammes.name: Cross-sectional imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Explicit official GME directory category, one-year advanced clinical training across CT, MRI, US, PET/CT and multiple radiology divisions. No dedicated public curriculum page linked from the directory; not silently treated as a separate ACGME or ABR specialty.

officialProgrammes.name: Musculoskeletal imaging
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate one-year MSK imaging fellowship with advanced subspecialty training; ACGME has a separate MSK Radiology program category, but do not infer this exact BIDMC program’s accreditation without the programme page stating it.

officialProgrammes.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Tufts Medical Center
officialProgrammes.name: Neuroradiology
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: One-year ACGME-accredited clinical physician programme, described jointly with Tufts Medical Center. Public rotations include two-week blocks at Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary and Boston Children’s Hospital. ABR neuroradiology subspecialty certification/exam exists, with separate prerequisites.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One official BIDMC GME category page describes eight advanced clinical fellowship opportunities: abdominal imaging, Body MRI, breast imaging, cancer imaging, cardiothoracic imaging, cross-sectional imaging, musculoskeletal imaging and neuroradiology. They are preserved as separate institutional variants within this single assigned item, not deduplicated into one generic specialty curriculum. The public list is not an exhaustive national directory. BIDMC describes some pages explicitly as one-year ACGME-accredited; no unqualified accreditation claim is inferred for other tracks. The category is not a combined residency, generic board specialty, research-only appointment, or non-physician physics programme. Individual tracks may include research and teaching but have central clinical imaging roles. The directory does not list Nuclear Radiology, Pediatric Radiology, or Imaging Informatics fellowships; those are not represented as BIDMC programmes here.
sourceCaveats: ACGME site displayed 2026 requirements effective 2026-07-01; this does not verify accreditation of every BIDMC track.
ABR exam eligibility and certification rules change; this check is dated 2026-10-07, and individuals must verify current primary-board language.
The BIDMC directory pages are institutional programme descriptions, not an independent audit of current accreditation or a complete public curriculum.
This course has not received human clinical review. A self-study answer key is not medical advice, validated assessment, or diagnosis.

No source image or patient record is copied into course files. Linked clinical case details are used solely to establish a case exercise; all learners must consult the source page and honor page-level licensing.

sourceReferences.title: BIDMC Radiology Fellowships directory
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official institution directory lists the eight fellowship opportunity labels; BIDMC identifies Harvard Medical School affiliation, clinical hands-on setting.

sourceReferences.title: BIDMC Radiology GME fellowships overview
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Lists advanced fellowship areas and describes clinical care, research, teaching; abdominal and neuroradiology are specifically described as ACGME-accredited one-year programmes.

sourceReferences.title: BIDMC Abdominal Imaging & Interventions Fellowship
sourceReferences.claimSupported: One-year ACGME-accredited physician fellowship; public rotations, clinical service, procedure education, didactics, evaluation and eligibility statements.

sourceReferences.title: BIDMC Neuroradiology Fellowship
sourceReferences.claimSupported: One-year ACGME-accredited clinical physician fellowship; Tufts/MEEI/Boston Children’s rotations, curriculum, conferences and scope of procedures.

sourceReferences.title: ACGME Radiology Program Requirements, FAQs and Applications
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Current requirements portal lists ACGME Diagnostic Radiology, Abdominal Radiology, IR, MSK, Neuroradiology, Nuclear Radiology, Pediatric Radiology and Clinical Informatics program categories; 2026 requirements effective July 1, 2026.

sourceReferences.title: ABR Get Certified in Diagnostic Radiology
sourceReferences.claimSupported: ABR DR eligibility depends on prior clinical year, accredited four-year residency or approved alternate pathway, exams, valid license and ethics; fellowship itself is not DR certification.

sourceReferences.title: ABR Get Certified in Subspecialties
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Current ABR radiology subspecialty options include neuroradiology, nuclear radiology, pediatric radiology and pain medicine; subspecialty eligibility requirements and exams are separate from fellowship completion.

sourceReferences.title: ABR 2026 Remote Qualifying (Core) Exam Guide
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official exam preparation guide; exam content covers broad DR/IR-DR domains and ABR warns that external prep resources do not necessarily align in type/scope.

sourceReferences.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public topic-indexed, current evidence-based imaging appropriateness materials spanning breast, cardiac, GI, MSK, neurologic, pediatric, systemic oncology, thoracic, urologic, vascular and interventional imaging.

sourceReferences.title: Undergraduate Diagnostic Imaging Fundamentals
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Publicly downloadable University of Saskatchewan textbook by Brent Burbridge and Evan Mah, CC BY-NC-SA, chapters across imaging fundamentals and anatomy/body systems; introductory rather than fellowship-level.

sourceReferences.title: Diagnostic Radiology Physics: A Handbook for Teachers and Students
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Free IAEA PDF (2014) covers imaging physics, dosimetry, instrumentation, quality, modality-specific topics, radiation biology/protection; copyright remains IAEA, permission required for reproduction.

sourceReferences.title: Radiopaedia Terms of Use
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Radiopaedia terms warrant contributed image content is de-identified and genuine; educational reuse is conditional on applicable CC BY-NC-SA and per-case exclusions, and bulk scraping/reuse is prohibited.

sourceReferences.title: Radiopaedia case: Lung cancer associated with a cystic airspace
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Example of a public, multi-modality longitudinal clinical imaging case; the case page includes source disclosures, clinical timeline, case DOI and study links. Link/view only.

sourceReferences.title: Diagnostic Radiology Resident Core Lecture Series
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Free AUR R&E Foundation supported curriculum states 20–30 minute lectures and nine subspecialty collections; no runtimes individually audited here, so excluded from verified hours.

sourceReferences.title: ACR Manual on Contrast Media
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official ACR page links the current manual, notes chapters updated in 2025, and states the reaction cards were last updated September 2026.

sourceReferences.title: IAEA Diagnostic Radiology Physics teaching slides
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official IAEA page lists 24 chapter slide decks and explains their relation to the Diagnostic Radiology Physics handbook; includes CT, ultrasound, MR, patient dosimetry, optimization, and protection.

sourceReferences.title: Stanford MSK Radiology Education
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official Stanford MSK page points learners to publicly available educational videos; a candidate YouTube transcript was accessible, but its exact public player runtime could not be verified, so it was not counted.
