medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is comparing radiographs, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and PET/CT. Which statement best captures an important interpretation principle?

options.text: Each modality measures different physical properties and has distinct strengths and limitations.
All modalities depict tissue density on a common scale.
PET uptake establishes histology.
MRI is always the most appropriate cross-sectional examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiography/CT, MRI, ultrasound, and PET use different physical signals. The clinical question and technical context determine how findings are interpreted; no one modality is universally best and PET uptake is not histology.

practiceQuestions.stem: An abdominal CT request does not state the clinical question. Which next step best supports a defensible protocol?

options.text: Select a routine multiphase protocol for every abdomen.
Clarify the clinical question and align coverage, dose, and contrast timing to it and local protocol.
Add all contrast phases to eliminate uncertainty.
Avoid checking prior imaging because it may bias interpretation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Protocol design depends on indication, coverage, dose, phases, and contrast timing. Extra phases do not universally improve the study and can increase exposure. Supervising/local protocol guidance remains essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A teaching MRI example shows a focus with different signal across sequences. What is the soundest initial approach?

options.text: Treat signal as sequence-dependent and review the full protocol, anatomy, and artifacts.
Interpret every bright focus as edema.
Infer a specific histology from one sequence alone.
Ignore sequence parameters because images are standardized.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Signal depends on sequence, tissue properties, acquisition, and artifacts; single-sequence brightness is not a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional emergency teaching scenario, a learner notices possible acute diffusion restriction. What is the best report-level reasoning?

options.text: Describe location and diffusion/ADC pattern, check the rest of the examination and context, and communicate urgent findings through local policy.
Call it a confirmed infarct without checking ADC or alternatives.
Make a treatment decision from the educational module.
Omit it unless the learner can name a single cause.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Board-style cognitive preparation emphasizes localization, sequence correlation, differential and communication. Imaging patterns are not a substitute for clinical decision-making or institutional supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public imaging case has a limited ultrasound window due to body habitus and bowel gas. How should this limitation affect the interpretation?

options.text: State the technical limitation and avoid claiming the exam excludes findings it could not adequately assess.
Report the examination as normal because no abnormality was seen.
Infer the unseen anatomy is normal.
Use the limitation as proof of a specific disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A study’s technical adequacy limits the conclusions it can support. Report limitations and consider appropriate follow-up in the clinical context through supervising practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A single FDG-avid focus is shown on a teaching PET/CT. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Uptake must be interpreted with anatomy, physiologic distribution, technical factors, and clinical context; it does not establish histology.
Any focal uptake proves malignancy.
A negative FDG study excludes all cancers.
PET/CT is interchangeable with post-therapy imaging for every radiopharmaceutical.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDG uptake can be physiologic, inflammatory, technically affected, false positive or false negative. Tracer and clinical context matter; imaging cannot by itself provide tissue diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which mapping of named classification systems is correct?

options.text: PI-RADS: prostate; LI-RADS: liver in defined contexts; renal cystic mass assessment uses a separate system.
PI-RADS: liver; LI-RADS: prostate.
All three systems apply to renal masses.
They are interchangeable universal malignancy scores.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These classification lexicons are organ- and context-specific. Avoid cross-applying them and verify the current edition and indications before clinical use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A breast-imaging learner sees a freely viewable educational case. What is the best use in this independent course?

options.text: Link to the case, verify current rights/disclosures, and use it for description and reasoning without copying/rehosting its images.
Assume free-to-view means unlimited public reuse.
Remove the case attribution and copy images.
Treat a case label as permission to provide unsupervised care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing does not grant blanket rights. The course links authentic cases only, respects page-level license and disclosure conditions, and does not reproduce images or patient records.

practiceQuestions.stem: A serial chest case shows a previously thin-walled cystic airspace that later changes morphology. What is the strongest cognitive takeaway?

options.text: Comparison with priors can reveal meaningful change; describe it and construct a context-based differential without generalizing one case.
Every cystic airspace is cancer.
A single old image is always more reliable than serial imaging.
The case can be used as a universal screening rule.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The linked case is an authentic longitudinal example with biopsy confirmation, but a single case cannot establish prevalence or a universal rule. The transferable skill is detecting change and communicating it.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about BIDMC’s directory category “Radiology Fellowships” is accurate?

options.text: It groups distinct clinical fellowship tracks; it is not one ABR board specialty or one uniform accredited curriculum.
All listed tracks necessarily have separate ABR exams.
Every track is publicly documented as ACGME-accredited.
A research component means the programme is research-only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BIDMC lists multiple advanced tracks with differing public pages and accreditation details. ACGME accreditation must be verified for each programme and ABR certification/examination status is distinct. No nuclear radiology fellowship is on the BIDMC list.

title: Adult Infectious Diseases Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship; independent board-oriented self-study course-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician-level prior knowledge comparable to internal medicine residency: physiology, microbiology, pharmacology, pathology, and clinical epidemiology. This is a recommendation for course comprehension, not an admission credential.
Working knowledge of specimen collection, diagnostic-test characteristics, antimicrobial classes and adult medicine; refresh foundational gaps with the linked OpenStax reading.
Ability to read current clinical guidelines and interpret uncertainty. No real patient records or protected examination materials are required.
objectives: Construct syndrome- and host-aware infectious-disease differentials and select tests with explicit reasoning.
Interpret microbiology, susceptibility reports and imaging/findings in context, including contamination and colonization.
Reason about antimicrobial selection, resistance, toxicity, interactions, pharmacokinetics, stewardship, source control, and OPAT using current authoritative guidance.
Apply board-blueprint coverage across bacteria, HIV, antimicrobial therapy, viral/fungal/travel disease, immunocompromised hosts, vaccines, infection prevention, and noninfectious mimics.
Analyze TB, HIV, transplant/oncology, STI, healthcare-associated and outbreak scenarios using current public-health resources.
Communicate recommendations and uncertainty in a concise consult note, handoff, and evidence appraisal.
Identify gaps in evidence and recognize that course assessments are formative, not a competence or passing predictor.

units.title: Approach to infection, host response, and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Build a time-ordered problem representation from host, exposure, syndrome, tempo, and severity.
Choose tests using pretest probability, specimen quality, test characteristics, and turnaround.
Distinguish colonization, contamination, latent infection, and active disease.
units.topics: Core microbiology, host defense, epidemiology; diagnostic stewardship; interpretation of cultures, antigen/antibody, molecular assays and pathology.
units.casePractice: Use fictional fever-and-culture vignettes to list top hypotheses, one discriminator, and a safe next diagnostic step.
units.assessment: One-page problem representation and test-selection justification; scoring rubric below.

units.title: Antimicrobial pharmacology, susceptibility, stewardship, and OPAT
objectives: Infer likely drug class from mechanism and spectrum; identify major toxicity/interactions and renal/hepatic adjustment flags.
Interpret susceptibility data in the clinical and source-control context, recognizing breakpoints and resistance mechanisms.
Perform a documented antibiotic time-out: indication, source, microbiology, de-escalation, route, duration, and monitoring.
units.topics: Antimicrobial Therapy (9%); PK/PD concepts; antibiogram limitations; resistance; outpatient parenteral therapy; antimicrobial stewardship.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional culture/AST table; compare empiric vs definitive strategy without prescribing for a real person.
units.assessment: Stewardship note scored for evidence/source control, organism-drug match, resistance nuance, harms, and reassessment.

units.title: Bacterial disease and invasive syndromes
objectives: Compare differential and initial evaluation for bacteremia, endocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, abdominal, bone/joint, skin/soft-tissue and urinary syndromes.
Interpret gram stain and culture with specimen, site, host, and timing.
Explain source control and when diagnostic uncertainty warrants escalation or consultation.
units.topics: Bacterial Diseases (27%); organisms and syndrome mapping across gram-positive/negative, anaerobes, spirochetes, mycobacteria, and atypicals.
units.casePractice: Fictional blood-culture timeline; map possible source, repeat/confirm testing and urgent escalation triggers.
units.assessment: Two-step case oral-board outline: identify dangerous alternatives, tests, and reassessment.

units.title: Tuberculosis and mycobacterial disease
objectives: Differentiate TB infection from disease and select appropriate diagnostic modalities by clinical question.
Apply airborne precautions and public-health coordination to suspected infectious pulmonary TB.
Summarize contemporary drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB recommendations from current primary guidance.
units.topics: Bacterial Diseases; mycobacteria; infection prevention and control; TB/HIV interaction.
units.casePractice: Public CDC case-study or fictional scenario: exposure timeline, isolation decision, specimen plan, and reporting pathway; no treatment order.
units.assessment: TB differential and infection-control memo with date of accessed guideline and uncertainty.

units.title: HIV: diagnosis, prevention, initial care, and ART
objectives: Select confirmatory testing and baseline evaluation; explain linkage, prevention, and non-stigmatizing counseling.
Compare principles for initial ART and recognize interaction/resistance issues; use current living NIH guidance rather than memorized static regimens.
Interpret virologic response and outline evaluation of suspected failure.
units.topics: HIV Infection (15%); epidemiology, testing, prevention, pathogenesis, ART, malignancy and comorbidities.
units.casePractice: Use publicly available AETC teaching slides or a fictional treatment-choice scenario; re-check current live guidance before answers.
units.assessment: Guideline citation exercise and ART decision map; no personalized real-patient therapy.

units.title: HIV-associated opportunistic infections and IRIS
objectives: Use immune status, prophylaxis, exposure, imaging/labs and disease tempo to compare key OI possibilities.
Distinguish OI-directed therapy from ART timing; identify potential immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
Use NIH adult/adolescent OI living guidance and note the last revision.
units.topics: HIV Infection (15%); OIs across bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, parasites and viruses.
units.casePractice: Review AETC indolent lung infection teaching slides as a linked case; do not copy the slides/images.
units.assessment: Case comparison matrix: evidence for/against differentials and guideline link, not a diagnosis claim.

units.title: Viral disease, hepatitis, respiratory pathogens, and emerging infections
objectives: Compare diagnostic windows and test interpretation for common viral syndromes and hepatitis.
Describe infection prevention, vaccination, risk communication, and escalation for emerging/high-consequence infections.
Use current authoritative source and recognize evidence changing with new variants/outbreaks.
units.topics: Viral Diseases (7%); HIV; vaccines; internal medicine/pulmonary overlap.
units.casePractice: Create a fictional travel/exposure viral-syndrome triage map with public-health contact point; no case images.
units.assessment: Short evidence appraisal using dates and public-health scope.

units.title: Fungal and parasitic disease; travel/tropical medicine
objectives: Use geography, season, exposure, host, and immune status to build a targeted differential.
Compare test modality and limitations for invasive fungal disease, parasitosis, and travel-associated febrile illness.
Identify high-consequence syndromes requiring urgent consultation and public-health coordination.
units.topics: Fungi (5%); Travel and Tropical Medicine (5%); selected bacterial/viral overlap.
units.casePractice: Fictional fever-after-travel timeline; select discriminating tests and isolate/report considerations.
units.assessment: Differential table scored on exposure reasoning, test choice, and red-flag recognition.

units.title: Transplant, oncology, neutropenia, and immunocompromised host
objectives: Classify risk by immunosuppression, transplant type/time, malignancy therapy, prophylaxis, and donor/recipient factors.
Develop a differential for febrile neutropenia and transplant-related infection using syndrome and timeline.
Integrate competing infectious and noninfectious causes while coordinating multidisciplinary care.
units.topics: Immunocompromised Host (Non-HIV) (5%); infection prevention; bacteria, fungi, viruses, parasites.
units.casePractice: Fictional post-transplant fever case; distinguish timeline-driven hypotheses; no patient records/images.
units.assessment: Timeline-based differential and handoff; rubric includes host factors and alternative etiologies.

units.title: Infection prevention, healthcare epidemiology, and outbreak response
objectives: Select isolation precautions by suspected transmission route and pathogen-specific recommendations.
Outline healthcare-associated infection surveillance, outbreak investigation, hand hygiene, disinfection/sterilization, and occupational exposure response.
Use denominators, case definitions, and bias awareness in simple epidemiologic analyses.
units.topics: Infection Prevention and Control (5%); Applied Epidemiology; outbreak investigation.
units.casePractice: CDC applied-epidemiology training case or fictional line-list exercise.
units.assessment: Outbreak memo with case definition, denominator, control steps, and data limitations.

units.title: Vaccination, prevention, STI, hepatitis, and counseling
objectives: Apply adult immunization schedules and distinguish live/non-live vaccine considerations under immunosuppression.
Use current CDC STI guidance, screening and partner-care frameworks with non-stigmatizing history-taking.
Synthesize prevention strategy, risk communication, and jurisdiction-specific reporting/partner services.
units.topics: Vaccinations (4%); HIV prevention; Viral Diseases; Infection Prevention and Control.
units.casePractice: Fictional preventive-care visit with risk-based questions and follow-up needs; no identifiable data.
units.assessment: Prevention plan citations and shared decision-making script, graded for completeness and respectful language.

units.title: Consultation practice, safety, evidence appraisal, and board-style synthesis
objectives: Deliver a concise consult presentation, prioritize time-sensitive threats, communicate uncertainty, and construct a safe follow-up plan.
Critically appraise guideline quality, scope, currency, conflicts, and limits of external validity.
Answer original single-best-answer clinical vignettes with explicit reasoning and identify distractor errors.
units.topics: Consult communication, safety, evidence appraisal, board-style retrieval and systems-based practice.
units.casePractice: Capstone fictional consult: write a handoff with timeline, problem list, recommendations for supervising review, and public-health steps.
units.assessment: Timed formative set plus reflective error log; not validated and not a passing predictor.

assignment.title: Longitudinal infectious-disease consult portfolio
tasks: For each of 12 fictional cases, submit a concise problem representation, prioritized differential, and test interpretation with limitations.
Prepare two antimicrobial time-outs and one current-guideline comparison; date-stamp every guideline consulted.
Complete one outbreak line-list interpretation, one HIV/OI case map, one travel-associated fever differential, and one transplant/oncology host-risk timeline.
Submit an end-of-course reflection identifying three reasoning errors caught and what source would correct each.
assignment.passingRule: No passing score asserted; local instructor may use rubric formatively. A rubric result is not clinical competence, board readiness, certification, or licensure.

assessment.format: Open-resource formative questions, case reasoning notes, and assignments mapped to the January 2026 public ABIM blueprint.
components: Eight to twelve original single-best-answer items with answer rationales.
Unit case assignments and guideline currency audit.
Capstone consult/handoff and self-directed retrieval review.
assessment.limits: Not official ABIM exam content, not psychometrically validated, not a predictor or guarantee of examination performance, and not a substitute for supervised clinical assessment.

unitMap.text: Approach to infection, host response, and diagnostic reasoning
Antimicrobial pharmacology, susceptibility, stewardship, and OPAT
Bacterial disease and invasive syndromes
Tuberculosis and mycobacterial disease
HIV: diagnosis, prevention, initial care, and ART
HIV-associated opportunistic infections and IRIS
Viral disease, hepatitis, respiratory pathogens, and emerging infections
Fungal and parasitic disease; travel/tropical medicine
Transplant, oncology, neutropenia, and immunocompromised host
Infection prevention, healthcare epidemiology, and outbreak response
Vaccination, prevention, STI, hepatitis, and counseling
Consultation practice, safety, evidence appraisal, and board-style synthesis

topicGaps: The verified specialty ledger now contains 48.328889 unique hours, exceeding the 36.0-hour target by 12.328889 hours. This is recorded viewing time, not supervised clinical training or evidence of board readiness.

A public Norton Infectious Diseases Institute Grand Rounds playlist supplies the 79 added recordings. Its topic mix is broad but varies in audience, depth, date, and format; the playlist is not a complete fellowship curriculum or an official Johns Hopkins didactic archive.

No dedicated, public, free HIV clinical lecture was verified in the added playlist. HIV is 15% of the January 2026 ABIM blueprint; ART, OI, testing, resistance, and prevention therefore remain dependent on current NIH/UW sources and the original written course content. The scripted HIV episode is not a recording and adds zero video hours.

The 5% ABIM non-HIV immunocompromised-host domain remains only partially taught by the public recordings; there is no comprehensive recording covering transplant, oncology, neutropenia, prophylaxis, and noninfectious complications together. The scripted host-risk episode is not a recording and adds zero video hours.

The recordings sample bacterial syndromes, fungi, parasites, respiratory viruses, antimicrobial therapy, diagnostics, vaccination, and infection prevention; they do not exhaust the organisms and clinical syndromes in the ABIM blueprint. In particular, complete pathogen-specific HIV/OI, fungal, travel, transplant, and 18% internal-medicine/noninfectious coverage is not established by runtime alone.
All authored episodes remain scripted, not rendered or published. Existing pilot and original clip-plan target minutes remain production plans, not available or verified lecture hours.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship; independent board-oriented self-study course
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) Infectious Disease subspecialty certification examination
ABIM Internal Medicine certification (prerequisite for the ABIM Infectious Disease certification pathway)
medical.boardStatus: A separate ABIM subspecialty certification examination in Infectious Disease exists. ABIM requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification, satisfactory accredited fellowship training, clinical competence and licensure; its current published policy specifies at least 24 total months including 12 full-time clinical months, and no required procedures. Johns Hopkins labels its Adult Infectious Diseases fellowship ACGME-accredited. ACGME requirements effective 2026 specify a 24-month ID program. Verify each rule with ABIM/ACGME at application; this independent course is not board-eligible training.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Educational self-study does not grant ABIM eligibility. Eligibility depends on prerequisite certification, accredited training, clinical competence, licensure and current ABIM policy. No course, videos, MCQs, or certificate can confer board eligibility or guarantee a pass.

officialProgrammes.name: ACGME Adult Infectious Diseases Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a 2–3-year physician fellowship, with first year focused on clinical training and later years primarily research/scholarly activity. Published first-year work includes JHH and Bayview consults, transplant/oncology ID, AIDS Care, microbiology and outpatient subspecialty clinics; the page gives typical consult-service time and named electives. Published conferences include core curriculum, case presentations and ID management conference. This page is not a public recording archive or a complete official lecture syllabus.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet initially cited a legacy directory URL; source verification used the current Johns Hopkins Division of ID fellowship pages above. Johns Hopkins also lists Pediatric ID as a separate division/program, a case-by-case adult/pediatric combined pathway using the adult page, and Transplant and Oncology ID (TOID) as ACGME-equivalent. These are preserved as distinct institutional offerings, not silently merged into this adult clinical board track. TOID is not treated as an independent ABIM board specialty/exam. Hopkins also describes possible joint clinical pharmacology and medical microbiology training; neither changes this track’s board identity. No Harvard variant was identified in the supplied single-program packet; this item is specifically the Johns Hopkins adult fellowship.
sourceCaveats: The Johns Hopkins public page describes local program design and examples; its public didactic calendar does not expose the complete internal curriculum or all recorded lectures. No proprietary course recordings are represented as available.
The public ACGME 2026 PDF is effective in 2026; apply the version in force on the relevant date. ABIM policy controls certification eligibility and can change.
ABIM blueprint percentages are the current January 2026 public specification retrieved; actual exam content can vary and should be checked for revisions.
The CDC STI page consulted calls the 2021 STI guideline its most current broad guideline; separately posted product availability information is newer. Check linked source updates before clinical use.

No physician, institutional faculty, or independent clinical reviewer has reviewed this educational course. The source research and public video metadata were checked but do not validate clinical decisions.

This independent study course confers no Johns Hopkins/Harvard affiliation, accreditation, graduate medical education, licensure, board eligibility, procedural competence, or certification. It cannot assure passing any examination.

topicGaps: The verified specialty ledger now contains 48.328889 unique hours, exceeding the 36.0-hour target by 12.328889 hours. This is recorded viewing time, not supervised clinical training or evidence of board readiness.

A public Norton Infectious Diseases Institute Grand Rounds playlist supplies the 79 added recordings. Its topic mix is broad but varies in audience, depth, date, and format; the playlist is not a complete fellowship curriculum or an official Johns Hopkins didactic archive.

No dedicated, public, free HIV clinical lecture was verified in the added playlist. HIV is 15% of the January 2026 ABIM blueprint; ART, OI, testing, resistance, and prevention therefore remain dependent on current NIH/UW sources and the original written course content. The scripted HIV episode is not a recording and adds zero video hours.

The 5% ABIM non-HIV immunocompromised-host domain remains only partially taught by the public recordings; there is no comprehensive recording covering transplant, oncology, neutropenia, prophylaxis, and noninfectious complications together. The scripted host-risk episode is not a recording and adds zero video hours.

The recordings sample bacterial syndromes, fungi, parasites, respiratory viruses, antimicrobial therapy, diagnostics, vaccination, and infection prevention; they do not exhaust the organisms and clinical syndromes in the ABIM blueprint. In particular, complete pathogen-specific HIV/OI, fungal, travel, transplant, and 18% internal-medicine/noninfectious coverage is not established by runtime alone.
All authored episodes remain scripted, not rendered or published. Existing pilot and original clip-plan target minutes remain production plans, not available or verified lecture hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinically stable adult has no urinary symptoms. Two properly collected cultures grow the same bacterium. There is no pregnancy and no planned endoscopic urologic procedure involving mucosal trauma. Which principle best guides management?

options.text: Treat every positive culture to prevent bacteremia
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in this setting; assess for a separate clinical indication
Use the longest available antibiotic course
Repeat cultures weekly until sterile

practiceQuestions.rationale: IDSA guidance recommends against screening/treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in most nonpregnant adults, including many older adults; the named exceptions matter. A positive culture alone is not infection. Re-check current guideline details and patient context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hospitalized adult is receiving broad empiric antibiotics. At the 48-hour review, cultures are negative, imaging shows no new focus, and the patient is improving. What is the most appropriate stewardship action?

options.text: Automatically continue the broadest agents for 14 days
Reassess whether infection remains likely, evaluate cultures and source-control information, then stop, narrow or continue with a documented rationale
Add a second broad agent to prevent resistance
Keep therapy unchanged because improvement proves bacterial infection

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured antibiotic time-out reassesses indication, syndrome, data, source control, choice, route and duration; improvement alone neither establishes bacterial cause nor justifies indefinite therapy. Current IDSA guidance is organism-specific and should not be replaced by a fixed rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: A laboratory reports an organism resistant to a commonly used agent, but the sample was collected from a nonsterile site and the patient has no matching syndrome. What is the key next reasoning step?

options.text: Treat the resistance result regardless of clinical context
Determine whether the organism represents infection, colonization, or contamination and assess specimen quality and syndrome fit
Assume the result proves invasive infection
Discard the result without checking the patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: Microbiology results require interpretation by site, specimen quality, host and clinical syndrome; resistance data guide therapy only when a clinically significant infection is established.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with cough, weight loss and an upper-lobe infiltrate is being evaluated for pulmonary tuberculosis. Which action should occur while diagnostic testing proceeds?

options.text: Use routine contact precautions only
Place in airborne infection isolation and coordinate testing/reporting with infection prevention and public health according to local rules
Wait for culture confirmation before isolation
Use droplet precautions only

practiceQuestions.rationale: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires prompt airborne infection control and public-health coordination; diagnostic testing and local policies determine next steps. Do not wait for culture confirmation to protect others.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an adult newly diagnosed with HIV, a learner needs current recommendations for initial ART and interactions. Which source is the best starting point?

options.text: A fixed regimen memorized from a decade-old lecture
Current NIH adult/adolescent antiretroviral living guideline and its linked drug interaction resource
An unsourced social-media post
A treatment algorithm for children

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIH guideline panels update adult/adolescent ART advice and direct readers to current interaction resources. Recommendations can change; the course blueprint is not a therapeutic protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with advanced HIV develops new inflammatory symptoms after pathogen-directed treatment and ART initiation. Which concept belongs in the differential while the learner reassesses the patient and alternative diagnoses?

options.text: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, without assuming it explains all deterioration
ART-associated immune recovery makes infection impossible
Resistance is proven by any new symptom
Stop all antiretroviral therapy automatically

practiceQuestions.rationale: IRIS is an important possibility in context, but new symptoms require reassessment for untreated/progressive infection, other diagnoses and guideline-directed decisions; automatic cessation is not justified by the concept alone. Consult current NIH OI/ART guidance and supervising clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: A returning traveler has fever. Which feature should most strongly shape the initial differential and diagnostic plan?

options.text: Travel destination and dates, specific activities/exposures, incubation timing, immune status, and illness severity
Only the country of citizenship
A routine broad test panel unrelated to the exposure history
The assumption that every post-travel fever is malaria

practiceQuestions.rationale: Travel-associated reasoning depends on geography, timing, activities/exposures, host factors, severity, and time-critical diagnoses; avoid anchoring on a single pathogen. Use current country-specific public-health guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A neutropenic patient receiving cancer therapy develops fever. Which reasoning approach is most defensible for an educational case?

options.text: Treat all fever as a noninfectious drug effect
Integrate degree/duration of immune suppression, timing, possible source, severity, local protocols and prompt senior/clinical-team escalation
Wait for all cultures before assessing urgency
Assume one organism is present in every neutropenic fever

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neutropenic fever can be time-critical and requires protocol-based clinical evaluation; this educational item tests risk recognition and escalation rather than supplying patient-specific orders. Differential includes infectious and noninfectious causes.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects the adult infectious disease exam blueprint retrieved for this curriculum?

options.text: HIV is the largest content category
Bacterial diseases account for 27%; HIV for 15%; internal medicine/noninfectious syndromes for 18%
All content areas have equal weight
Procedural competence is the only assessment domain

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABIM January 2026 blueprint lists bacterial diseases 27%, HIV 15%, internal medicine/noninfectious 18%, antimicrobial therapy 9%, and the other published percentages. The board may revise its blueprint.

practiceQuestions.stem: A resident proposes counting a freely viewable educational video as permission to place its clinical images in a new course. What is the best response?

options.text: Public viewing automatically grants unlimited reuse rights
Link to the source and verify a reuse license/permissions before copying or rehosting any images or slides
Remove the source attribution and reuse it
Assume de-identification eliminates copyright

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not a rehosting license, and de-identification does not extinguish copyright. This curriculum links to source material and copies no images or patient records.

title: Categorical Medical Genetics Residency Program
level: Clinical physician residency; independent self-study curriculum, not a residency-aligned independent study

prerequisites.audience: Physicians/residents or advanced graduate learners with medical genetics and genomic science foundations; the course is not a substitute for medical school or prerequisite accredited clinical training.
requiredKnowledge: Human biology, cell biology, molecular biology and basic inheritance
Clinical history-taking, differential diagnosis and basic laboratory interpretation
Statistics and critical appraisal of clinical evidence
Professional familiarity with consent, confidentiality and referral pathways
prerequisites.accessibility: Independent online self-study via public links where available. No patient care, clinical rotation, supervised counseling, laboratory sign-out or procedures are included.

objectives: Construct a structured phenotype and family history, articulate a differential and recognize uncertainty.
Select among genetic testing modalities conceptually based on the clinical question and assay limitations.
Interpret variant classifications and genomic reports using evidence hierarchy, not single-source inference.
Recognize core dysmorphology, biochemical, pediatric, adult, cancer, prenatal and neurogenetics domains.
Communicate limits, consent, privacy and results responsibly; distinguish screening, diagnostic testing and risk assessment.
Map curriculum topics to ABMGG published general and Clinical Genetics and Genomics blueprint domains without implying exam prediction.
Distinguish categorical physician residency from combined tracks, laboratory specialties, research fellowships and physician board certification.

topicGaps: Six new unique recordings add 5.3992 observed hours. Eight unique public recordings now total 6.5147 hours against the 36-hour video floor; 29.4853 hours remain unfilled. No planned/scripted episode is included in this total.

Public long-form lecture coverage remains insufficient for dysmorphology and congenital anomaly reasoning, cytogenomic nomenclature/laboratory interface, contemporary variant-classification and report-conference depth, prenatal/reproductive genetics, broad pediatric neurodevelopmental assessment, and longitudinal consultation/QI. New recordings are uneven and should be used as focused supplements rather than as a complete board-domain sequence.

Older recordings are historical teaching, not current clinical policy. The 2014 metabolic webinar, 2020 newborn-screening and oncology webinars, 2022 adult-neuro webinar, and vendor-produced content require current-source cross-checking; local newborn-screening panels and protocols vary.

The five original teaching episodes are source-grounded scripts, not rendered or reviewed videos. The remaining target is a feasibility gap, not a claim that scripts or proposed target minutes supply actual video hours.

boardNames: American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ABMGG): Clinical Genetics and Genomics initial certification examination (separate physician specialty board exam).
ABMGG General Examination: published general blueprint content relevant to specialty training; the specialty exam pathway is governed by ABMGG requirements.
medical.boardStatus: This item is the actual Johns Hopkins Categorical Medical Genetics Program, an ACGME-accredited four-year directory listing. ABMGG identifies Clinical Genetics and Genomics as a physician specialty with its own certification examination. ABMGG pathways require a minimum prior year of accredited residency/direct patient care followed by two years of accredited medical genetics residency, or the specified dual-board approved combined training pathway. The course itself is not accredited training and does not confer exam eligibility. ABMGG also lists Clinical Biochemical Genetics and Laboratory Genetics and Genomics laboratory specialties and Medical Biochemical Genetics/Molecular Genetic Pathology pathways separately; these are not bundled into the categorical physician course. The Johns Hopkins page separately lists combined IM, Pediatrics, MFM and REI tracks; not merged into this categorical curriculum. No categorical track-specific exam distinct from ABMGG Clinical Genetics and Genomics certification was found.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a constructed family, a disease-associated variant is labeled VUS in a laboratory report and is not supported by segregating data. What is the most appropriate educational interpretation?

options.text: Treat the VUS as the diagnosis because it is rare
Use it as the sole basis for predictive testing in unaffected relatives
Do not use VUS status alone for clinical decisions; seek phenotype/evidence review and future reassessment
Reclassify it as pathogenic because it is in ClinVar

practiceQuestions.rationale: A VUS is uncertain and should not direct medical management. Variant interpretation integrates evidence and clinical context; an archive entry does not automatically settle classification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A well-phenotyped fictional child has developmental delay and congenital anomalies after initial evaluation. Which statement best describes exome/genome sequencing?

options.text: It always identifies the cause
It may be considered early in the diagnostic pathway under guideline criteria, but has limitations and may yield uncertain or secondary findings
It replaces clinical evaluation and counseling
A negative result excludes genetic disease

practiceQuestions.rationale: Professional guidance supports considering ES/GS early in selected children, but methods have limitations, and negative results do not exclude genetic etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A positive newborn screening result for a metabolic condition means:

options.text: The infant has a confirmed disorder
A screen-positive result needs prompt follow-up and confirmatory evaluation under the relevant system
No follow-up is needed if the newborn appears well
Only DNA sequencing can confirm it

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening identifies risk; it is not equivalent to a diagnosis. Follow the applicable state/program protocol and qualified clinical pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public ClinVar record lists conflicting submissions with different review statuses. What should the learner do?

options.text: Assume the majority vote is correct
Treat all records as expert panel consensus
Inspect evidence, submitter, review status, condition match and date; do not treat aggregation as independent adjudication
Ignore clinical phenotype

practiceQuestions.rationale: ClinVar archives submissions and highlights evidence/conflicts, but does not independently curate or resolve all assertions.

practiceQuestions.stem: An apparently unaffected parent carries an autosomal dominant disease variant reported in an affected child. Which concept can explain this without excluding the variant?

options.text: Reduced penetrance or age-dependent expression may be relevant
It proves sample mix-up
The variant must be benign
Autosomal dominant variants always cause identical phenotype

practiceQuestions.rationale: Penetrance and expressivity vary; family phenotype and ascertainment require careful review rather than categorical inference.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which result most clearly separates cytogenomic copy-number assessment from balanced rearrangement detection?

options.text: A microarray can detect many copy-number changes but generally does not detect balanced rearrangements without dosage change
Karyotype detects all nucleotide substitutions
FISH excludes all genome-wide variants
A negative microarray excludes genetic disease

practiceQuestions.rationale: Array methods evaluate dosage and can miss balanced structural rearrangements; method selection depends on the clinical question and lab capabilities.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hereditary cancer scenario includes an affected family member available for testing. A key principle is:

options.text: Tumor-only findings always establish an inherited germline variant
Testing an affected relative may be more informative for familial risk assessment; tumor and germline testing answer different questions
Family history is unnecessary once a panel is ordered
Negative testing eliminates all familial risk

practiceQuestions.rationale: Affected-relative testing may clarify a familial hypothesis; somatic tumor findings are not automatically germline. A negative result may be uninformative.

practiceQuestions.stem: An asymptomatic adult with a concerning family pattern seeks a risk estimate. The best initial genetics work-up emphasizes:

options.text: A three-generation pedigree with verified diagnoses/ages and a clear referral question
Only a direct-to-consumer test
A precise probability from one vague family story
Presuming the same diagnosis across relatives

practiceQuestions.rationale: Family history detail, diagnosis verification and a defined question are foundations; individual risk estimates require context and current qualified evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A prenatal screening assay indicates elevated probability of a chromosomal condition. The most accurate communication is:

options.text: This is a confirmed fetal diagnosis
Screening estimates risk; discuss confirmatory diagnostic options, limits and patient preferences
The fetus is unaffected until proven otherwise
Only postnatal testing matters

practiceQuestions.rationale: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing are different. Counseling should preserve informed choice and explain test limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A candidate molecular finding is absent from population databases and computational tools predict damaging effects. What is missing for a robust interpretation?

options.text: Nothing; absence plus prediction automatically proves pathogenicity
Integrated evidence across gene-disease validity, phenotype, segregation, technical validity and calibrated variant criteria
A social media poll
Proof the patient has a rare disease

practiceQuestions.rationale: Population rarity and in-silico evidence alone do not establish causality; assess evidence strength and independence in context.

title: Clinical Biochemical Genetics Fellowship
level: ACGME-accredited postdoctoral clinical laboratory specialty fellowship (MD/DO/eligible PhD; not physician-only)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Foundational biochemistry and molecular genetics, including pathway/enzyme logic and Mendelian inheritance.
Graduate-level familiarity with laboratory methods, analytical validity, statistics and specimen handling; clinicians also need relevant medical genetics context.
Learners should have appropriate professional education for their role. This course is advanced independent education, not an entry-level clinical qualification.
objectives: Relate biochemical pathways to the marker patterns and limitations used in inherited metabolic disease evaluation.
Interpret newborn-screen findings as screening results and formulate appropriate confirmatory questions.
Compare analytic methods used in amino acids, organic acids, acylcarnitines, sterols and selected enzyme/biomarker assays.
Integrate biochemical, molecular and phenotype data with uncertainty and differential diagnoses.
Explain quality assurance, preanalytics, validation, reporting and professional laboratory responsibilities.
Map study to all 15 approximate ABMGG blueprint domains without implying exam prediction.

units.title: Biochemical genetics practice, pathways, and test stewardship
objectives: Draw a pathway-to-marker map for disease groups and connect pathway blocks with expected analytes.
Differentiate a screening result from diagnostic evidence; select confirmatory testing and explain its limitations.
topics: Preanalytical variables; analyte/ratio patterns; screening vs diagnosis; phenotype-first approach; interpretation uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional positive newborn screen to select a timely confirmatory panel, call-out triggers, and communication steps.
units.assessment: Submit an analyte/pathway concept map with one caveat per inference.

units.title: Amino-acid disorders and nitrogen disposal
objectives: Interpret amino acid patterns across PAH/BH4 defects, MSUD, tyrosinemia, glycine encephalopathy and sulfur-amino-acid disorders.
Use ammonia, glutamine, citrulline, arginine, orotic acid and amino acid context to compare UCDs without overcalling a single marker.
topics: PAH/Phe/Tyr; pterin cofactors; branched chain amino acids; homocysteine and remethylation; glycine; serine; UCD biochemistry.
units.casePractice: Interpret fictional plasma amino-acid results and identify alternate/secondary patterns requiring confirmatory evaluation.
units.assessment: Pattern table: result, pathway, differential, confirmatory test, and limitation.

units.title: Urea-cycle disorders and hyperammonemia reasoning
objectives: Map enzyme/transporter blocks to nitrogen and amino-acid patterns.
Recognize elevated ammonia as time-sensitive and explain immediate escalation, sample integrity, and parallel testing principles.
Compare primary UCDs with organic acidemias, liver dysfunction and secondary hyperammonemia.
topics: CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1, NAGS; glutamine/citrulline/arginine; orotic acid; collection issues; crisis pathway; chronic guideline scope.
units.casePractice: Tabletop case with rising ammonia: give prioritized differential, who to call, needed parallel samples, and acknowledge local emergency protocol.
units.assessment: Grading requires no medication or dialysis dose; tests urgency, pattern recognition, and escalation.

units.title: Organic acidemias, ketone disorders, and cofactors
objectives: Interpret urine organic-acid and acylcarnitine patterns for propionic/methylmalonic acidemias, isovaleric acidemia, GA1 and selected ketone disorders.
Identify B12/cobalamin and other cofactor-sensitive differential patterns; distinguish pathway clues from confirmation.
topics: Organic acids; MMA vs PA; C5/C5OH; 3-MCC; ketogenesis/ketolysis; cobalamin; biotin; molybdenum; folate; pyridoxine; pterins.
units.casePractice: Interpret an invented acylcarnitine/urine-organic-acid result set and draft a differential and orthogonal test plan.
units.assessment: Scored on pattern matching, confounders and not making genotype or treatment claims from one test.

units.title: Fatty-acid oxidation, lipids, sterols and bile acids
objectives: Interpret fasting/illness context and acylcarnitine patterns across short-, medium- and long-chain oxidation defects.
Distinguish a profile-based suspicion from confirmatory enzyme/molecular evidence.
Map cholesterol/bile acid and selected lipid disorders to laboratory clues.
topics: MCAD/VLCAD/long-chain; MADD; hyperlipidemia; cholesterol; Smith-Lemli-Opitz; NPC; bile acids; newborn-screen follow-up.
units.casePractice: Pattern exercise comparing acylcarnitines with illness, nutrition and sample timing; explain false-positive/false-negative considerations.
units.assessment: One-page algorithm assessed for context, interpretation, and no false certainty.

units.title: Carbohydrate metabolism and glycosylation
objectives: Compare glycogenoses, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, galactose/fructose and congenital glycosylation disorders by pathway and test approach.
Choose a laboratory strategy appropriate to phenotype and analyte stability.
topics: GSD (Pompe cross-reference to lysosomal unit); glycolysis; gluconeogenesis; galactose; fructose; CDG; pentose phosphate.
units.casePractice: Case conference: translate a fictional fasting-triggered phenotype and screening marker into differential and confirmatory assays.
units.assessment: Oral-style explanation scored on pathway coherence and test choice.

units.title: Lysosomal, sphingolipid and storage disorders
objectives: Relate enzyme, substrate, biomarker and molecular methods in major lysosomal disorders.
Recognize pseudodeficiency, overlapping phenotypes, specimen requirements and confirmatory testing needs.
topics: MPS I/II/III/IV/VI/VII; Gaucher; Fabry; GM2; Krabbe; Niemann-Pick; GM1; mucolipidosis; Pompe; cystinosis; NCL.
units.casePractice: Use a de-identified open case report or ACMG action sheet; propose a differential and confirmation plan; do not reuse article images.
units.assessment: Interpretive memo distinguishes screening biomarker, enzyme assay, and molecular confirmation.

units.title: Mitochondrial and energy metabolism disorders
objectives: Compare mitochondrial DNA, nuclear gene, respiratory-chain and maintenance defects in clinical-laboratory evaluation.
Interpret lactate and other metabolic markers in preanalytical and clinical context.
topics: Mitochondrial myopathy; Leigh syndrome; adult presentations; electron transport/assembly; mtDNA variant/heteroplasmy; mtDNA maintenance.
units.casePractice: Review a fictional referral with elevated lactate and discuss preanalytical confounding, next test and differential.
units.assessment: Rubric weights confounder analysis and test sequence over named-disease recall.

units.title: Peroxisomal, purine/pyrimidine, transport, creatine, neurotransmitter and metal disorders
objectives: Compare targeted metabolites and assays for peroxisomal disorders, purine/pyrimidine defects, transport, creatine and neurotransmitter disorders.
Select relevant metal or trace-element testing when phenotype supports it.
topics: Peroxisomal disorders; uric acid/purines/pyrimidines; amino-acid transport; creatine biosynthesis/transport; neurotransmitters; metals.
units.casePractice: Construct a diagnostic matrix from phenotype to specimen/analyte to confirmatory methods, with pitfalls.
units.assessment: Assessment requires each rare domain mapped with appropriate limits.

units.title: Laboratory platforms, QA and test validation
objectives: Compare chromatography, GC-MS, tandem MS, stable-isotope methods and enzymatic assays by analyte and analytic limitations.
Apply QC, calibration, proficiency testing, method verification/validation, reference intervals and result reporting concepts.
topics: Amino-acid chromatography; GC-MS organic acids; LC/GC-MS; tandem MS; isotope methods; enzyme assays; specimen integrity; QA/QC; regulatory/validation principles.
units.casePractice: Audit a fictional method change using analytic performance, comparability, validation, QC, and communication rubric.
units.assessment: Laboratory memo scores analytic validity, clinical validity and interpretive clarity.

units.title: Newborn screening systems, counseling and interprofessional communication
objectives: Explain screening purpose, positive predictive value, follow-up urgency and jurisdiction-specific panels.
Communicate uncertainty and escalation needs to clinicians/families with scope-aware language.
Integrate nutrition, clinical genetics and laboratory roles.
topics: NBS systems; ACT sheets; follow-up; consent and communication; metabolic dietitian; family-centered care; age transitions; reproductive context.
units.casePractice: Draft a call note for an abnormal screen, separating observed result, differential, requested next steps, and emergency escalation per local protocol.
units.assessment: Communication rubric: accurate, timely, non-alarmist, no definitive diagnosis before confirmation.

units.title: Integrated biochemical case conference and board-domain synthesis
objectives: Integrate biochemistry, phenotype, lab quality, confirmatory testing and uncertainty into concise case reasoning.
Explain laboratory findings to a multidisciplinary audience and identify evidence limitations.
Use the official blueprint to self-audit domain coverage without inferring passing probability.
topics: All 15 ABMGG domains; report interpretation; case conference; uncertainty; ethical use of de-identified cases; lifelong updates.

unitMap.text: Amino-acid disorders and nitrogen disposal

unitMap.text: Urea-cycle disorders and hyperammonemia reasoning

unitMap.text: Organic acidemias, ketone disorders, and cofactors
coveredTopics: Organic acids; MMA vs PA; C5/C5OH; 3-MCC; ketogenesis/ketolysis; cobalamin; biotin; molybdenum; folate; pyridoxine; pterins.

unitMap.text: Fatty-acid oxidation, lipids, sterols and bile acids

unitMap.text: Carbohydrate metabolism and glycosylation
coveredTopics: GSD (Pompe cross-reference to lysosomal unit); glycolysis; gluconeogenesis; galactose; fructose; CDG; pentose phosphate.

unitMap.text: Lysosomal, sphingolipid and storage disorders

unitMap.text: Mitochondrial and energy metabolism disorders

unitMap.text: Peroxisomal, purine/pyrimidine, transport, creatine, neurotransmitter and metal disorders

unitMap.text: Laboratory platforms, QA and test validation

ABMGG Clinical Biochemical Genetics specialty certification examination (distinct from Medical Biochemical Genetics subspecialty examination; shared Medical/Clinical Biochemical Genetics content blueprint)
medical.boardStatus: A separate ABMGG Clinical Biochemical Genetics specialty examination exists; ABMGG also has a distinct Medical Biochemical Genetics subspecialty examination, and the board publishes a shared Medical/Clinical Biochemical Genetics content blueprint. As of 2026-10-07, the next listed Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics exam cycle is 2027; those exams are offered in odd-numbered years. ABMGG requires passing the General exam plus a specialty exam for diplomate status. Hopkins says successful program completion makes trainees eligible to sit, but individual credential/degree requirements remain board-controlled; Hopkins misspells ABMGG as AMBGG. This independent course grants no eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABMGG states an MD, DO, or qualifying PhD is required for Clinical Biochemical Genetics; completion of accredited training is necessary but individual eligibility depends on board review. A separate and distinct Medical Biochemical Genetics physician subspecialty requires one accredited year after Clinical Genetics and Genomics residency. This is not the same fellowship. Do not infer combined-program status or eligibility from this independent curriculum.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital; Biochemical Genetics Laboratory at Kennedy Krieger Institute
officialProgrammes.name: Clinical Biochemical Genetics Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Directory currently labels this distinct Clinical Biochemical Genetics fellowship ACGME accredited and two years. Detailed public page describes a 24-month postdoctoral laboratory-training program; methods include amino-acid chromatography, GC-MS organic acids, tandem-MS acylcarnitines, sterol GC-MS, stable-isotope methods, newborn screening exposure, lab QA, case conference, journal club, didactics, supervised result interpretation and clinic observation. Patient assignment/metabolism call are conditional on prior clinical-genetics training and institutional credentialing. The page is nested under research/postdoctoral fellows but describes formal accredited clinical laboratory training, not a research-only or non-physician supplement. It accepts doctoral-track categories; it is not a physician-only fellowship.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet contained one official institutional variant: Johns Hopkins. Hopkins has a separate one-year Medical Biochemical Genetics fellowship; ABMGG defines it as a physician clinical subspecialty for prior Clinical Genetics and Genomics diplomates. That separate programme is not merged into this MED-083 track. The assigned item is a genuine specialty-track program, not a combined program or generic directory-only category. No Harvard variant was identified in the supplied packet; no global search beyond the supplied Hopkins source was represented as complete. The 2026 ACGME requirements are program standards, not the Hopkins curriculum; the Hopkins page supplies local published curriculum details.
sourceCaveats: The Johns Hopkins directory calls Clinical Biochemical Genetics ACGME accredited and two years; the formal ACGME requirements confirm a 24-month program. Johns Hopkins’ detailed page describes local objectives and experiences but is not a guaranteed current day-to-day schedule.
The Hopkins directory page has an apparent “AMBGG” typo. ABMGG is the correct official certifying board acronym.

ABMGG Clinical Biochemical Genetics is a separate lab specialty credential/exam. Medical Biochemical Genetics is a distinct clinical subspecialty requiring clinical genetics residency and is not merged into this track.
ACGME training exposure and Hopkins hands-on work require supervision and competency assessment. Online resources cannot supply such experiences.

Clinical Biochemical Genetics is not physician-only; qualifying PhD holders may be eligible subject to ABMGG rules. Clinical direct-care duties described by Hopkins are conditional on clinical genetics training and credentialing.

topicGaps: No candidate media had both independently observed public runtime and verified no-login free access in this run.

ACMG blueprint coverage remains to be supplied by new, recorded, runtime-probed original videos: amino acids; organic acids; cofactors; carbohydrates; lipids; lysosomes; mitochondria; peroxisomes; purines/pyrimidines; transport; creatine; neurotransmitters; metals; laboratory; other disorders.
The 2026 specialist seminar catalogue is a useful topic map but video sessions are locked/priced or login-gated and are excluded from free external hours.
A small number of candidate YouTube pages appeared in search, but public metadata extraction encountered HTTP 429/403 or a sign-in anti-bot challenge; no bypass was attempted.

No additional recording met all inclusion criteria: direct playback publicly accessible without login/payment, substantively relevant to this fellowship, and runtime observed from a primary media/player source. Verified new recording count remains 0; no added external hours.

APHL and New England Consortium offer promising newborn-screening archive leads, but the directory pages do not establish individual no-login playback plus exact runtime. NEC-linked YouTube requests encountered extraction/bot barriers; no challenge bypass or cookies were used.
MetabERN advertises relevant expert video modules, but access requires degree submission and staff validation; it is excluded rather than counted as free public viewing.

The four original scripts address introductory laboratory reasoning and selected urea-cycle, elevated-C3, and lysosomal interpretation. They do not fill the remaining 36-hour video floor and leave substantial board-domain teaching gaps: broad amino-acid disorders, full organic-acid/cofactor coverage, carbohydrate/glycosylation, fatty-acid oxidation/lipids/sterols, mitochondrial and peroxisomal disease, purine/pyrimidine, transport, creatine, neurotransmitters, metals, and extensive laboratory methods/QA.
