practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional newborn has a positive screening result for elevated phenylalanine. Which statement is the most accurate next interpretive step?

options.text: The screen alone proves PAH deficiency.
Treat the screen as a referral signal and arrange timely diagnostic evaluation, including quantitative amino acids and evaluation for relevant differential causes.
Urinary phenylketones alone definitively establish diagnosis.
Wait for symptoms before confirmation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A screen is not a definitive diagnosis. The differential includes persistent hyperphenylalaninemia and disorders of pterin metabolism; confirmatory biochemical/genetic assessment is needed. Exact follow-up follows current local protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional patient with severe hyperammonemia, the team is considering a urea-cycle defect. Which interpretive statement is best?

options.text: A single citrulline value identifies every UCD.
Ammonia must be interpreted with amino acids and other biochemical findings; urgent escalation and local emergency pathways are essential.
Normal liver enzymes exclude UCD.
Wait for sequencing before escalating care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patterns including citrulline, arginine, glutamine and urine orotic acid can help discriminate defects, but single markers do not diagnose all disorders. A suspected hyperammonemic crisis is urgent; this learning material gives no treatment dose or substitute protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has elevated C3 acylcarnitine and increased methylmalonic acid. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The profile uniquely establishes propionic acidemia.
Consider methylmalonic acidemia and cobalamin-related differential diagnoses; correlate urine organic acids, clinical context and confirmatory studies.
Methylmalonic acid excludes an inherited disorder.
A normal newborn screen rules it out at any age.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A biochemical pattern directs differential and further testing rather than uniquely diagnosing from one analyte. Cobalamin processing defects and acquired factors are relevant.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional ill infant has a profile concerning for fatty-acid oxidation disease. Which context is most useful for cautious interpretation?

options.text: Only the family’s stated diagnosis.
Feeding/fasting and illness state, specimen timing/quality, the whole acylcarnitine pattern, and confirmatory testing.
One borderline marker is sufficient for final genotype assignment.
A normal glucose permanently excludes all FAO disorders.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Metabolite patterns depend on context and screening is not confirmatory. A robust interpretation uses the profile, circumstances, and appropriate confirmatory assays/genetics.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABMGG blueprint category has the largest approximate percentage among the listed categories in the August 2025 Biochemical Genetics blueprint?

options.text: Amino acids (15%)
Laboratory (8%)
Creatine (1%)
Peroxisomes (3%)

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published approximate percentages list amino acids at 15%, followed by lipids at 13%, organic acids and lysosomes at 12% each. Percentages are approximate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A laboratory observes a positive lysosomal enzyme screen. Which response best reflects biochemical genetics test stewardship?

options.text: Report definitive disease without considering pseudodeficiency or sample issues.
Consider phenotype, sample quality, assay-specific limits, substrate/biomarker and appropriate orthogonal or molecular confirmation.
Ignore the result because enzyme assays are never useful.
Use a normal value from another assay platform without validation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening or enzyme results require analytical and clinical interpretation; pseudodeficiency and assay-specific context can matter. Confirmation is disease- and method-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician requests an interpretation of a raised lactate from a poorly documented collection. What is the best laboratory response?

options.text: Call mitochondrial disease confirmed.
Explain collection/processing limitations, correlate with clinical context, and recommend repeat/confirmatory evaluation when indicated.
Treat the result as proof of a respiratory-chain defect.
Discard all clinical information.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lactate is nonspecific and vulnerable to preanalytical confounding. The result should be contextualized; no isolated value confirms a mitochondrial diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the two Johns Hopkins biochemical-genetics offerings is correct?

options.text: Clinical Biochemical Genetics and Medical Biochemical Genetics are the same one-year physician pathway.
Clinical Biochemical Genetics is a two-year ACGME lab specialty track; Medical Biochemical Genetics is a distinct one-year clinical subspecialty following Clinical Genetics and Genomics training.
Neither has a separate ABMGG examination.
Both are generic directory labels with no accredited status.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins separately lists a two-year Clinical Biochemical Genetics program and a one-year Medical Biochemical Genetics fellowship. ABMGG similarly separates the lab specialty from a physician-only subspecialty.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the legal/educational status of a linked published case report in an open PMC article?

options.text: Openly readable means every image may be copied into course materials.
Link to the article for learning; do not rehost images/records, check article-specific license before reuse, and preserve de-identification.
Patient images can be copied if names are omitted.
A single published case establishes a standard protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free access is not blanket reuse permission. Keep authentic patient resources linked and respect licensing/privacy; one case report is not a protocol or generalizable evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: What do ACGME requirements and Johns Hopkins public program description support about training duration and experience?

options.text: An independent 36-hour online curriculum qualifies a learner for laboratory sign-out.
The accredited training is 24 months with substantial supervised lab experience, patient exposure and didactics; an online course cannot substitute for this.
The ACGME mandates exactly 36 hours of recorded lectures.
Completion guarantees board certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME describes a 24-month supervised postdoctoral training program with minimum laboratory and patient/didactic experiences. The independent course confers no hands-on competence, accreditation or board eligibility.

title: Combined MFM Fellowship and Medical Genetics Residency
prerequisites: Physician-level prior learning: medical degree and completion of OB/GYN residency-level core knowledge; designed for advanced residents/fellows, faculty, and genetics/MFM board review.
Foundational competence in obstetrics, prenatal care, embryology, genetics, statistics, and evidence appraisal.
Not an entry-level medical-school course; course completion confers no supervised patient-care or procedural competence.
objectives: Distinguish screening from diagnostic testing and appropriately describe residual uncertainty.
Integrate fetal phenotype, family history, assay limits, and current guidelines into a structured differential.
Compare genetic testing modalities and explain indications, limitations, and consent issues.
Appraise maternal-fetal medicine and clinical-genetics evidence and map learning to current board-blueprint domains.
Communicate results in a non-directive, inclusive, patient-centered, and uncertainty-aware manner.
Coordinate multidisciplinary diagnostic and perinatal planning without claiming clinical competence.

units.title: Foundations: inheritance, genome architecture, and phenotype
objectives: Construct a three-generation pedigree and distinguish dominant, recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial, de novo, and mosaic mechanisms.
Use phenotype chronology and family history to formulate—not declare—a genetic differential.
Explain variable expressivity, penetrance, pleiotropy, imprinting, and parent-of-origin effects at a level needed for prenatal consultation.
topics: Chromosome/gene structure, meiosis, mosaicism, imprinting and UPD
Phenotype descriptors, dysmorphology, family history and ancestry-sensitive risk assessment
boardDomains: ABMGG Clinical I multiple malformations/dysmorphology (16%), XXIV molecular mechanisms/genomics (8%), XXIII population genetics (1%); ABMGG General I–VI; ABOG MFM clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Use a fictional pedigree of recurrent pregnancy loss and a fetal anomaly to identify three competing inheritance models and tests that would discriminate them.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page pedigree, prioritized differential, and explanation of which missing family details could change counseling.

units.title: Reproductive screening and informed choice
objectives: Distinguish population screening from diagnostic testing and explain sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and prevalence effects.
Compare cfDNA, serum/ultrasound screening, carrier screening, and diagnostic pathways without describing a screen as a diagnosis.
Counsel neutrally about opting in or declining; document the limits and possible incidental findings.
topics: Common aneuploidies, opt-in sex chromosome screening, microdeletion/genome-wide screening limits
Carrier screening, residual risk, reproductive options and values-sensitive counseling
boardDomains: ABMGG XX Reproductive Genetics (7%), XIX Diagnostic techniques (11%), XXII Ethical/legal (1%); ABOG MFM prenatal care/fetal diagnosis (official blueprint page is dynamic and not publicly extractable here)
units.casePractice: Work through a fictional screen-positive trisomy 21 cfDNA result and a separate no-call result; name the confirmatory options and counseling checkpoints.
units.assessment: Complete a comparison matrix and record a two-minute standardized patient explanation using plain-language screening-versus-diagnosis distinctions.

units.title: Prenatal diagnostic methods and variant interpretation
objectives: Select between karyotype, targeted testing, chromosomal microarray, and sequencing based on the clinical question.
Explain test resolution, limitations, uncertain/secondary findings, and maternal-cell contamination risks.
Apply ACMG/AMP-style variant classification concepts without overcalling uncertain variants.
topics: CVS and amniocentesis specimens and timing as clinical decisions requiring current local guidance
Karyotype, FISH, QF-PCR, CMA and their scope
Panel, exome/genome sequencing, coverage gaps and phenotype-based prioritization
CNV, mosaicism, placental mosaicism, VUS and secondary/incidental findings
boardDomains: ABMGG XIX diagnostic techniques (11%), XX reproductive genetics (7%), XXIV molecular/genomics (8%); ABOG MFM prenatal diagnosis
units.casePractice: Compare three fictional fetal test reports for a structural anomaly: a normal karyotype, pathogenic CNV with phenotype match, and VUS; write a limitations statement for each.
units.assessment: Test-selection memo scored for fit to indication, limitations, informed consent, and correct non-diagnostic language.

units.title: First-trimester ultrasound, anatomy, and genetics
objectives: Organize a gestational-age-aware structural phenotype using standard imaging reports.
Recognize when an ultrasound finding changes the differential or prompts diagnostic testing rather than screening alone.
Describe technical limitations and avoid diagnosing an anomaly from a single unclear image.
topics: Dating, plurality, chorionicity, nuchal translucency context and early structural survey
CNS, cardiac, abdominal wall, skeletal and multisystem phenotypes
Image quality, view completeness, gestational timing and referral
Phenotype-to-genotype hypothesis generation and differential expansion
boardDomains: ABMGG I multiple malformations/dysmorphology (16%), XIX diagnostics (11%), XX reproductive genetics (7%); ABOG MFM fetal diagnosis/ultrasound reasoning
units.casePractice: Review the linked SMFM educational case page if its current image/content loads; otherwise use a fictional narrative-only phenotype. Do not save or reproduce any case image.
units.assessment: Submit a structured phenotype summary, differential list ranked by evidence, and diagnostic next-step options.

units.title: Procedural diagnosis, fetal risk, and laboratory pathway
objectives: Compare CVS and amniocentesis as diagnostic sampling pathways and state that procedure decisions require clinician-patient discussion.
Explain what a placental sample can and cannot establish, including confined placental mosaicism considerations.
Design a specimen-to-laboratory workflow with consent, identity checks, contamination controls, and result communication.
topics: CVS/amniocentesis distinctions and current institutional procedure standards
Placental versus fetal genotype; mosaicism and discordant findings
Sample selection, maternal-cell contamination, turnaround expectations and laboratory coordination
Diagnostic test choice driven by phenotype, family history, gestational age, and informed preferences
boardDomains: ABMGG XIX diagnostics (11%), XX reproductive genetics (7%), XXII ethics (1%); ABOG MFM fetal diagnosis and procedural counseling
units.casePractice: Create a fictional flow diagram for a patient who elects invasive prenatal testing after a structural anomaly; include questions for the lab and safeguards against sample mix-up.
units.assessment: Workflow rubric: clinical question alignment 25%, consent 25%, sample/quality safeguards 25%, limitations and follow-up 25%.

units.title: Fetal anomaly patterns, dysmorphology, and differential diagnosis
objectives: Synthesize multiple anomalies into syndrome-level and non-syndromic differentials.
Distinguish chromosomal, copy-number, monogenic, teratogenic, infectious, multifactorial, and deformation/disruption hypotheses.
Prioritize tests with an explicit rationale and retain uncertainty when phenotype overlaps.
topics: Congenital malformation patterns and skeletal dysplasia red flags
Teratogens, infections, fetal growth patterns, and non-genetic mimics
Phenotype-driven panel/exome escalation and multidisciplinary review
boardDomains: ABMGG I multiple malformations/dysmorphology (16%), IV skeletal dysplasias (1%), VI cardiovascular (4%), XIX diagnostics (11%); ABOG MFM fetal anomaly assessment
units.casePractice: In a fictional fetus with increased nuchal translucency and later cardiac/renal findings, generate at least four plausible etiologic classes and justify staged testing.
units.assessment: Oral-board-style differential presentation scored for breadth, prioritization, evidence and calibrated uncertainty.

units.title: Prenatal exome/genome sequencing and rare disease
objectives: Identify cases in which sequencing may add value after standard diagnostic workup.
Explain phenotype-driven analysis, trio testing, VUS/secondary findings, consent, and evolving evidence.
Avoid presenting published diagnostic yield as an individual patient probability or guarantee.
topics: ACMG/Genetics in Medicine guidance on fetal exome sequencing
Cases with structural anomalies after nondiagnostic chromosome testing
Trio sequencing, phenotype updates, variant classification and reanalysis
Limitations: technical coverage, uncertain variants, incidental findings, counseling burden
boardDomains: ABMGG XIX diagnostics (11%), XXIV molecular mechanisms/genomics (8%), I multiple malformations (16%), XXII ethics (1%); ABOG MFM prenatal diagnosis
units.casePractice: Use a fictional multisystem anomaly phenotype to write an exome referral question, consent issues, and a plan if a VUS is returned.
units.assessment: One-page test-order rationale graded for indication, prior testing, counseling, uncertainty, and result follow-up.

units.title: Fetal growth restriction and genetic investigation
objectives: Apply SMFM Consult #52 US definition of FGR and distinguish it from broader international terminology.
Identify when early FGR, anomaly, or polyhydramnios warrants offering diagnostic genetic testing under the cited guidance.
Interpret umbilical artery Doppler and surveillance recommendations in the context of current guideline text—not as independent treatment advice.
topics: FGR definition: EFW or AC below 10th percentile per SMFM
Early-onset FGR (<32 weeks), structural anomalies, polyhydramnios, CMA offer
Umbilical artery Doppler surveillance and guideline-specific delivery thresholds
Differential: placental, maternal, fetal, infectious and genetic contributions
boardDomains: ABOG MFM fetal growth/placental disorders; ABMGG XX reproductive genetics (7%), I multiple malformations (16%), XIX diagnostics (11%)
units.casePractice: Fictional 29-week pregnancy: EFW 7th percentile plus a structural anomaly. Identify which guideline supports offering CMA and list complementary maternal/placental/fetal evaluation questions.
units.assessment: Evidence table distinguishing screening, diagnostic test offer, surveillance and delivery guidance; cite source/date for each.

units.title: High-risk pregnancy and fetal-genetic intersections
objectives: Organize a differential for maternal disease, placental dysfunction, fetal disease, and multifetal complications.
Recognize that genetic findings may modify—but do not alone determine—pregnancy surveillance, delivery site, timing, or neonatal planning.
Integrate current, condition-specific guidelines rather than generalizing a single pathway.
topics: Hypertensive disease, diabetes, maternal comorbidity and placental disease as context
Twins/chorionicity, growth discordance, fetal anomalies and screening constraints
Preterm birth, fetal surveillance, fetal therapy referral and perinatal coordination
Genetic result interpretation across maternal, placental, and fetal genomes
boardDomains: ABOG MFM maternal medical complications, fetal/placental disorders, multifetal gestation, prematurity; ABMGG XX reproductive genetics and XIX diagnostics
units.casePractice: Build a fictional multidisciplinary case conference agenda for monochorionic twins with discordant growth and a cfDNA no-call; do not infer a diagnosis from the no-call.
units.assessment: Case conference handout graded for source use, clinical prioritization, counseling and handoffs.

units.title: Genetic counseling, ethics, law, and reproductive autonomy
objectives: Use non-directive, accessible and inclusive language, including the right to accept or decline screening/testing.
Explain uncertainty, incidental results, disability perspectives, and jurisdiction-sensitive legal context without coercion.
Identify confidentiality, family communication, privacy and equitable-access concerns.
topics: Prenatal screening/testing results and decision support
Confidentiality, secondary findings, disability ethics, reproductive autonomy
Date-sensitive law and referral to local institutional/legal resources; no general legal advice
boardDomains: ABMGG XXII ethical/legal principles (1%), XX reproductive genetics (7%); ABOG MFM professional practice/counseling
units.casePractice: Role-play a fictional consult in which the patient declines testing after counseling; document understanding without steering or pressure.
units.assessment: Counseling rubric: comprehension 25%, autonomy/non-directiveness 25%, uncertainty and test limits 25%, inclusive communication 25%.

units.title: Result disclosure, recurrence risk, and perinatal transition
objectives: Communicate positive, negative, uncertain, and inconclusive results with appropriate scope and residual-risk language.
Plan clinical genetics, MFM, fetal/neonatal, and laboratory follow-up around the patient’s goals and pregnancy context.
Explain recurrence risk as condition- and family-specific, not as a generic number.
topics: Result verification and coordination with the ordering team
Prenatal-to-postnatal diagnostic confirmation and phenotype update
Recurrence risk: inheritance, de novo event, mosaicism, parental testing and residual uncertainty
Birth planning and neonatal/family follow-up as multidisciplinary processes
boardDomains: ABMGG XX reproductive genetics (7%), XXII ethical/legal (1%), I multiple malformations (16%); ABOG MFM neonatal/perinatal coordination
units.casePractice: For a fictional pathogenic variant found prenatally, create a result-disclosure outline that avoids assuming severity or predetermined family choices.
units.assessment: Written communication graded for accuracy, uncertainty, next steps, recurrence caveats and non-directive tone.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, systems practice, and integrated board reasoning
objectives: Locate the current official guideline/board blueprint and distinguish program standards from board content.
Appraise evidence for population, test performance, applicability, uncertainty and update date.
Integrate genetic and MFM evidence into a defensible educational case answer while recognizing clinical review needs.
topics: Blueprint-based retrieval practice across reproductive genetics and broad clinical genetics
Guideline hierarchy and date checks; changing cfDNA guidance as case study
Interdisciplinary handoffs, quality assurance, access and diagnostic stewardship
No simulation of unsupervised clinical decisions or procedural competence
boardDomains: ABMGG clinical blueprint categories and ABOG MFM exam blueprint; no assertion of exact ABOG percentages because the current interactive blueprint page did not load publicly
units.casePractice: Cumulative fictional case: early FGR plus multiple anomalies, negative cfDNA, uncertain family history. Build a differential, testing plan, counseling points and guideline audit trail.

assignment.title: Capstone fictional multidisciplinary case conference
assignment.prompt: Analyze a fictional pregnancy with early-onset FGR, a structural finding, a nonreportable cfDNA screen, and a relevant family history. Build a differential and staged diagnostic options; specify what needs genetics/MFM/laboratory consultation; prepare a values-sensitive counseling outline and source/date audit trail. No real patient data, management directive, or imaging reproduction.

assignment.passThreshold: For educational self-assessment only; no validated board-prediction or competence threshold.

assessment.method: 12 unit formative submissions plus 10 original multiple-choice questions and capstone; answer rationales are supplied. Questions are original, not official exam items.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient’s cfDNA screen is high risk for trisomy 21, and the patient asks whether this confirms fetal trisomy 21. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Yes; cfDNA is a diagnostic test when it reports high risk.
It increases risk but is not diagnostic; offer counseling, detailed ultrasound, and discuss CVS or amniocentesis.
A normal ultrasound would make the screening result invalid.
Repeat cfDNA is required before any other discussion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG 2026 says a positive result should be followed by genetic counseling, detailed anatomic survey, and an offer of diagnostic testing. Screening is not diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A prenatal cfDNA result is nonreportable. Which interpretation best matches current ACOG guidance?

options.text: Treat as a negative result if no ultrasound anomaly is reported.
Offer counseling, comprehensive ultrasound evaluation, and diagnostic testing because a nonreportable result is associated with increased aneuploidy risk.
Diagnose trisomy 21.
Repeat the same screen and do not discuss diagnostic testing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 ACOG advisory states that nonreportable results should prompt counseling, comprehensive ultrasound evaluation, and offer of diagnostic testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the January 2026 ACOG advisory, which statement about general-population cfDNA microdeletion screening is correct?

options.text: Routine screening for any microdeletion is recommended.
Routine screening for any microdeletion is not recommended; patients seeking fetal CNV information should be offered diagnostic testing.
A positive microdeletion cfDNA result proves the fetal genotype.
Microdeletion screening replaces ultrasound.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACOG does not recommend routine general-population screening for microdeletions and advises diagnostic testing for those seeking fetal CNV information.

practiceQuestions.stem: SMFM defines fetal growth restriction (FGR) as which sonographic finding in Consult Series #52?

options.text: Estimated fetal weight below the 5th percentile only.
Estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference below the 10th percentile for gestational age.
Birth weight below the 10th percentile.
Abnormal middle cerebral artery Doppler alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SMFM Consult #52 defines FGR as EFW or AC below the 10th percentile. It is a prenatal definition.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional pregnancy has unexplained isolated FGR diagnosed at 30 weeks. Which diagnostic option does SMFM recommend offering?

options.text: Chromosomal microarray as prenatal diagnostic testing.
Routine toxoplasmosis, rubella, and herpes screening in all cases.
cfDNA as a diagnostic substitute for CMA.
No further testing because isolated FGR cannot be genetic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SMFM recommends offering prenatal diagnostic testing with CMA for unexplained isolated FGR diagnosed before 32 weeks. Routine toxoplasmosis, rubella, or herpes screening without other risk factors is discouraged.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fetus has a structural anomaly and a normal karyotype. Which test class is specifically suited to detecting submicroscopic copy-number gains and losses?

options.text: Chromosomal microarray, with counseling about its scope and uncertain findings.
Repeat cfDNA as definitive diagnosis.
Karyotype only, because it detects all CNVs.
No further testing can be considered.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CMA assesses copy-number variation beyond conventional karyotype resolution. Diagnostic scope and uncertain findings require counseling.

practiceQuestions.stem: After chromosomal microarray is nondiagnostic in a fetus with multiple structural anomalies, which statement about fetal exome sequencing is best supported by ACMG guidance?

options.text: It may be considered in selected cases with fetal anomalies after standard testing, with careful pretest counseling.
It should be used for every pregnancy as a population screen.
It guarantees a molecular diagnosis.
A variant of uncertain significance establishes a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACMG’s fetal exome points-to-consider document supports selective consideration when anomalies are present and standard evaluation is nondiagnostic; uncertainty and limitations must be disclosed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pregnant patient elects diagnostic testing after an abnormal ultrasound. Which is the best initial step in a learner’s plan?

options.text: Choose a test before clarifying the clinical question.
Clarify the phenotype, prior results, patient goals, and the test question; then discuss diagnostic options and limitations with the treating team.
Assume a cfDNA screen identifies all relevant causes.
Promise a definitive answer for all genetic disorders.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Test selection depends on indication and phenotype, and informed consent should cover the scope and limitations. No test provides universal exclusion of genetic disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes the institutional combined programme at Johns Hopkins?

options.text: A generic directory category with no clinical training.
A four-year combined MFM fellowship and Medical Genetics residency for physicians who have completed an ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency, with MFM and genetics training plus research.
A two-year standalone genetics fellowship that grants both board certifications automatically.
A non-physician research supplement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official Hopkins department page describes a four-year combined clinical programme for physicians after accredited OB/GYN residency; years include genetics, MFM, additional clinical training, and research. Board eligibility requires each board’s separate requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: What certification pathway applies to the combined training described by Hopkins and ABMGG?

options.text: One joint MFM-genetics board exam and one joint certificate.
Separate examinations/certifications through ABOG for MFM and ABMGG for Clinical Genetics and Genomics, subject to each board’s credentialing.
ABMGG certification alone automatically grants ABOG MFM certification.
No board certification exists for either specialty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMGG lists combined MFM/Medical Genetics training as a dual-board-approved pathway and says applicants must meet each board’s credentialing requirements; Hopkins names ABOG MFM and ABMGG Clinical Genetics examinations.
